The true believer, whose faith is sound, is one whose desire and inclination agree with the method of God, from which he does not deviate. The Truth, glory be to Him, has said: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted...﴾ 71 (Surat al-Mu'minun).

And His saying, Most High: ﴿and his affair has been [ways of] excess (furutan)﴾ 28 (Surat al-Kahf): that is, his affair was a loss and vain dust, as if he had wasted himself.

Almighty's saying: ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord..."﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29). That is: say, the truth has come from your Lord. He chose the word "Lord" (rabb) and did not say "from Allah," because everyone believes that the Lord is the One who created, as in His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created them, they would surely say, "Allah." So how are they turned away?﴾ (Surat al-Zukhruf: 87).

And His saying: ﴿And if you asked them who created the heavens and the earth, they would surely say, "Allah..."﴾ (Surat Luqman: 25).

So the meaning of ﴿from your Lord﴾ is: by your own acknowledgment. The One who created you, sustained you and cared for you is the One who sent down this truth to you. And ﴿your Lord﴾ means: not only my Lord, but your Lord and the Lord of all people.

Truth (al-haqq) is that which is firmly established, and since it comes from Allah, no one can change it. For whoever changes his word is one who decides a matter and then is ignorant of something that comes later, and then corrects himself. So the truth is from Allah, because nothing is hidden from Him, and nothing escapes His knowledge. Therefore, no one may object to any of His rulings from among His creatures.

Lordship (rububiyyah, the divine attribute of nurturing and sustaining) is a gift. Your Lord is the One who created you and supplied you with blessings, and He is the One who nurtures you as a father nurtures his child. For this reason, no one has objected to lordship. As for divinity (uluhiyyah, the right to be worshipped), its requirement is obligation: do this, and do not do that. So He addressed them with lordship, in which lies their benefit, and did not address them with divinity, which restricts their choices. A human being by nature does not incline toward that which restricts his choices, and so they turn to worshipping other gods, because those gods have no requirements.

So the one who worships the sun, or an idol, or anything else: what has his object of worship commanded you, and what has it forbidden you? Worship is nothing but the obedience of a worshipper to the one worshipped. Therefore they may say: "Yes, this is a god, and yes, this is a religion, because it leaves me free to do what I want."

For this reason, we find that those who claim divinity or claim prophethood always tend to lighten the religious laws, because they know that the heavenly laws are difficult for people, since they impose restrictions on their freedom of movement and freedom of choice. When Musaylimah claimed prophethood, he saw that people resented zakat, so he dropped it from them. Likewise, when Sajah claimed prophethood, she lightened the prayer. Otherwise, how would they gather people around them?

How similar the claimants of yesterday are to the claimants of today, who sell religion for a worldly price, issuing rulings to people that permit what Allah has forbidden, such as free mixing of the sexes and other matters, until the matter of religion has become trivial to people. Religion, although it is innate in the human soul, nevertheless a person inclines toward whoever lightens it for him. You are amazed when you see some intellectuals and holders of degrees going to charlatans and believing them, and you see one of them deceiving himself that he is following a religion that comforts him and lets him do whatever he wants under its shade.

So, since you believe in the lordship of creation and the lordship of sustenance and bounty, you must believe in what has come from your Lord, as we say in the proverb: "He who eats my bread listens to my word." Nevertheless, despite Allah's favor and blessings upon them, say to them: there is no compulsion in belief: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29), because the benefit of faith returns to you yourselves.

It has come in the hadith qudsi (a sacred hadith, whose wording is attributed to Allah): "Indeed, you will never be able to harm Me so as to harm Me, nor benefit Me so as to benefit Me. Even if the first of you and the last of you, the living of you and the dead of you, and the present of you and the absent of you were to gather upon the most pious heart of one man among you, that would not increase My dominion by anything. And even if the first of you and the last of you, the living of you and the dead of you, and the present of you and the absent of you were to gather upon the most wicked heart of one man among you, that would not decrease My dominion by anything."

"And even if the first of you and the last of you gathered in one open plain and each asked Me for what he wants, and I gave each one his request, that would not diminish what I have except as a needle diminishes the sea when one of you dips it into the sea. That is because I am Generous, Glorious, Noble. My giving is speech, and My punishment is speech. My command, when I desire a thing, is only that I say to it, 'Be,' and it is."

So the benefit of faith returns to the believer, as He said: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, it is for his own self, and whoever does evil, it is against it﴾ (Surat Fussilat: 46). But I love for My creatures to always be upon good, better than I am. I give them the good of this world, and I also love to give them the good of the Hereafter.

This verse came after His saying: ﴿And keep yourself patient with those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 28).

When the opponents of Islam saw the call spreading little by little, they tried to stop it, not by aggression against those who believed, but through the Prophet ﷺ himself. They sent a delegation to him, saying: "O Muhammad, we have sent to you so that we may present our excuse regarding you. You have brought upon your people what no one before you has brought. You have reviled our gods, belittled our minds, and cursed our religion. If you want wealth, we will gather wealth for you until you become the richest of us. If you want status, we will make you our leader. If you want kingship, we will make you king."

The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "By Allah, I do not have what you say. Rather, my Lord has sent me to you with the truth. If you obey, then it is for your benefit; if not, then Allah is my helper against you."

This attempt between them and him ﷺ was made in the hope that, when the matter is private, the Messenger of Allah might be lenient. When they did not achieve their aim, they said: "Let us seek intercession through someone you love, for perhaps he will be ashamed to accept from us, since we are his opponents. Let us send to him someone he loves." So they went to his uncle Abu Talib. When his uncle spoke to him, he said his famous words: "By Allah, O uncle, even if they placed the sun in my right hand and the moon in my left, on condition that I abandon this matter, I would not abandon it until Allah makes it manifest, or I perish defending it."

When this attempt also failed, they approached him from a third direction and said: "Let us arrive at a matter that is a middle ground between us and you: leave these poor people, turn your face away from them, do not tie yourself to them, and turn your face toward us." So Allah revealed:

﴿And keep yourself patient...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 28).

Then Allah, glorified and exalted, clarified that Islam, or the religion that Allah has sent down, does not take its rulings from the people to whom it was sent down, because the Messenger of Allah was only sent to establish for them the standards of truth and to call his people to them. How, then, could they set these standards, and command the Messenger of Allah to turn his face away from the poor and turn toward them?

Therefore He said: ﴿And say, "The truth is from your Lord..."﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29), because He sent me with the truth as a messenger to you, and I have come only to guide you. If you want me to direct myself according to your desires, then the matter has been reversed. Your request that I turn away from those who call upon their Lord morning and evening and face you instead shows that your belief is not sincere, and that you are not serious about following me. Therefore I have no need of you.

Then He, exalted, says: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29). That is: proceed on this basis, that every truth descends from Allah. It is not that I take the truth from you and then return it to you; rather, the truth with which Allah has sent me to you is the truth. On this basis: whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve.

The command in this verse has already been clarified by us, where we said: whenever we find a command that does not carry its intended meaning, we should understand that the command has been used in a place other than its proper one. As a father says to his neglectful son, "Play as you wish," he does not, of course, intend to command his son to play. Rather he intends to threaten and rebuke him. Likewise in: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe, and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29).

Otherwise, if the verse were taken in its literal sense, then whoever believes would be obeying the command, and so would the disobedient: ﴿So whoever wills, let him believe﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29) is obedience to the command, and ﴿and whoever wills, let him disbelieve﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29) is also obedience to the command.

Then both of them are obedient. How, then, would He punish one and not the other?

So the command here is not in its literal sense; it is for equalization and threat. That is: whether you believe or do not believe is all the same to Us; you are free in this matter, because the outcome of faith returns to you. Allah, exalted, is free of need of you and of your faith. Likewise, the creation of those who believed in Muhammad are also free of need of you. So Allah's independence of you is coupled with the independence of the Messenger, and Muhammad will be victorious, and the religion of Allah will spread without you.

Allah, exalted, willed that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ proclaim the call in Makkah and make it heard openly in the ears of the chieftains of disbelief and the tyrants of the Arabian Peninsula, whose opinion and command no one departs from, because they had status and leadership among the Arab tribes.

For a wisdom willed by Allah, exalted, the victory of Islam did not come through these people. Had victory come at their hands, it would have been said: they became accustomed to victory and to leadership over the Arabs, and they rallied fanatically around one of their own, so they could rule the entire world. Thus, partisanship for Muhammad did not create faith in Muhammad; rather, faith in Muhammad created partisanship for Muhammad.

Then Allah, exalted, says: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared for the wrongdoers a Fire whose enclosure will surround them﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29). The punishment here is for whoever chooses disbelief. But why does the verse emphasize and magnify the matter of punishment? Because informing people of the punishment, exaggerating it, and describing it in its horror serve as a warning, not so that people fall into the causes of punishment, but so that they refrain from the crime and keep away from its causes. Therefore, the vividness and the magnitude of punishment are a mercy from Allah toward His servants, because fear of punishment will prevent them from crime.

The meaning of ( أعتدنا ) [a'tadna, "We have prepared"] is: We have made ready. So the matter is settled in advance. Paradise and Hellfire are already created, prepared and equipped; they are not going to be prepared in the future. They were prepared by One who is capable and wise. Allah prepared Paradise to be wide enough for all creation if they believe, and He prepared the Fire to be wide enough for all creation if they disbelieve. If some of creation believe and some disbelieve, then whoever believed has freed up his place in the Fire, and whoever disbelieved has freed up his place in Paradise.

For this reason, Allah said concerning this matter: ﴿And that is Paradise, which you have been made to inherit for what you used to do﴾ (Surat al-Zukhruf: 72).

Thus, Allah's creation of Paradise and the Fire is a matter entirely regulated, and no crisis or crowding will ever occur in them; rather, each has its designated place. And His saying: ﴿for the wrongdoers﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29).

Wrongdoing (zulm) is taking a right and giving it to someone else. Wrongdoing has many forms, the most heinous and greatest of which is associating partners with Allah, because you take Allah's right of worship and give it to another. This is the pinnacle of wrongdoing. Then, any other wrongdoing short of that: every wrongdoer receives punishment according to the measure of his wrongdoing, unless he is a polytheist. The punishment of the polytheist is continuous and lasting, never ceasing or slackening. As for a believer who wrongs others short of shirk, he is punished for it, and then Allah admits him into Paradise, if he does not repent and if Allah does not forgive him.

His saying: ﴿whose enclosure will surround them﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29). The saradiq (enclosure, a tent or canopy), as we say today: "they set up the saradiq," meaning the tent. The meaning of saradiq is: that which encompasses them. It is as if Allah, exalted, pitched a tent over the Fire that surrounds them and confines them, so that their eyes cannot reach any place free of fire, because seeing a place free of fire might suggest to them hope of escape. Allah, exalted, wants to deprive them of hope of escape. Then He, exalted, says: ﴿And if they call for relief, they will be relieved with water like murky oil that scalds the faces. Wretched is the drink, and evil is the resting place﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29).

Istighathah (calling for relief) is the cry of pain from one who is suffering, to one who can remove that pain, as He said in another verse: ﴿I cannot help you, nor can you help me﴾ (Surat Ibrahim: 22). That is: when you cry out from the punishment, I cannot remove your cry, and likewise you cannot remove my cry.

So the people of the Fire, when they call for relief from the pain of punishment, the word (yughathu, "they will be relieved") leads the mind to think that they will be relieved by some mercy from Allah, that a breath of mercy will come to them, or that the punishment will be lightened for them. No.

﴿They will be relieved with water like murky oil﴾ (Surat al-Kahf: 29). That is: if they ask for relief with cool water that would ease the pain of the Fire, they will instead be given water like al-muhl.

Al-muhl is the sediment of boiling oil, which they call dardi, or it is molten metal such as lead and the like. This requires a heat higher than the boiling of water. Thus they increase in heat beyond the heat of the Fire, and they are punished from the very direction from which they expected mercy.

Allah's saying here: (yughathu, "they will be relieved") is an ironic style of expression, because the rule in linguistic styles is that you

Then He mentioned after it the ruling concerning the believers: ﴿Indeed, those who have believed and done righteous deeds—indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of anyone who does good work﴾ [18:30].

Let it be kept in mind that the Speaker is a Lord who is All-Wise; not a single letter of His speech is without a purpose, and behind it lies a wisdom. For when He spoke of faith, He made it a choice subject to the will of the servant, but He preferred that faith come first and precede disbelief. As for when He speaks of the ruling on each of the two, He began with the ruling on disbelief, on the basis that "the warding off of harm takes precedence over the attainment of benefit."

Here we observe that Glorified is He joined righteous deeds to faith, because faith is the creed from whose root conduct springs; there is no benefit in faith without action in accordance with that faith. The purpose of faith is to bind the command or prohibition to God in whom one has believed. Therefore the combination of faith and righteous deeds came in several places in the Book of God, among them His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿By time, indeed, mankind is in loss, except for those who have believed and done righteous deeds and advised each other to truth and advised each other to patience﴾ [103:1–3].

This is because when faith bears the fruit of righteous deeds among believers, they will inevitably be exposed to many hardships and difficulties that require mutual counsel to patience and mutual counsel to truth. We have an example in this matter in the Companions of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who bore the burden of the call and endured harm in the cause of their faith in God, Exalted is He.

Then He, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of anyone who does good work﴾ [18:30]. We observe that "man" (من) here is general, encompassing the believer and the disbeliever; therefore He, Glorified is He, did not say, "Indeed, We do not allow to be lost the reward of one who does good faith," because the worker who does good work may be a disbeliever, and yet God does not deprive him of his due, but gives him his share of recompense in this world.

So the disbeliever, if he strives and excels in knowledge, agriculture, or commerce, is not deprived of the fruit of his effort and striving; rather, it is hastened to him in this world, and the matter ends there, with no share for him in the Hereafter. He, Blessed and Exalted is He, says: ﴿And We will turn to what they did of deeds and make them scattered dust﴾ [25:23].

He, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Whoever desires the immediate [life], We hasten to him therein what We will, for whom We intend. Then We have made for him Hell; he will burn therein, blamed and banished﴾ [17:18].

He, Exalted is He, says: ﴿And those who disbelieved—their deeds are like a mirage in a level desert which the thirsty one thinks is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing; but he finds Allah there, and He pays him in full his account. And Allah is swift in account﴾ [24:39].

Those have received their wages in full, and taken their share in this world: varieties of bliss, praise, and commendation; their memory has been immortalized, and statues and celebrations have been erected for them. Therefore, in the Hereafter, he comes and finds nothing but regret and remorse, since he is confronted with the existence of a God in whom he did not believe. A person seeks his reward only from the one for whose sake he worked, and these did not work for God but for humanity, for society, and for fame; they have received all of that in this world, and nothing remains for them in the Hereafter.

(Those:) that is, those who believed and did righteous deeds: ﴿For them are Gardens of Eden﴾ [18:31].

The gardens (al-jannat): we have seen a picture of them in this world, and the term is used both in a technical (shar'i) sense and in a linguistic (lughawi) sense. As for the technical sense, it is the one we know: the abode that Allah the Exalted has prepared as the reward of the believers in the Hereafter. As for the linguistic meaning, it is the place that contains crops, fruits and trees which screen whoever walks among them and conceal him; the root j-n-n revolves entirely around concealment and hiddenness. Thus madness (junun) is the concealment of the intellect, the jinn (jinn) are creatures that are not seen, and janna (janna, a shield) is the armour that covers the body from the attacker... etc.

We have said that when the Truth, glorified is He, speaks to us of an unseen matter, He speaks to us with words that exist in our language. In the language we speak, the meaning exists first and then the word that indicates it exists. So when we know that this word is set for this meaning, then when the word is pronounced we understand its meaning. But if the things Allah tells us about are unseen, as the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "In it is what no eye has seen, no ear has heard, and no human heart has conceived,"

So from where do we bring the words that indicate these meanings, when we do not know them? For this reason the Truth, glorified is He, expresses them by what resembles them in our language, but gives them a description that distinguishes them from the garden of this world, as in His saying: ﴿The likeness of the Garden which the righteous have been promised: in it are rivers of water unaltered...﴾ [47:15].

We know the river and we know water, but His saying "unaltered" (ghayr asin) comes to distinguish the water of this world. Likewise in: ﴿rivers of wine, delicious to those who drink﴾ [47:15]: wine is known in this world, but it is not a delight to its drinker; he gulps it down quickly, because he cannot savour its taste or smell, just as you might drink a cup of juice in sips so that you enjoy its flavour and take pleasure in it. Moreover, the wine of this world beclouds the intellects, unlike the wine of the Hereafter. So when He gave it the name "wine" so that we would recognise it, He distinguished it by being a delight; the wine of this world is not like that. For our language does not contain the things that Allah will create for us in Paradise: "in it is what no eye has seen, nor ear heard." The eye's perceptions are fewer than the ear's perceptions, for the eye gives you only the scene you have seen, whereas the ear gives you the scene you have seen and that which others have seen. Then He says: "nor has it occurred to a human heart," thus widening the scope of what is in Paradise beyond what we are able to perceive. Likewise in His saying: ﴿and rivers of honey, purified﴾ [47:15].

We know honey, so He distinguished it here as "purified." It is well known that in earlier times people would take honey from the mountains, and pebbles and sand would stick to it; therefore He distinguished the honey of Paradise as purified. Likewise in His saying: ﴿among lote-trees without thorns﴾ [56:28]: we know the lote-trees of this world, which are a kind of tree with thorns, but the lote-trees of Paradise are not like that, for they are "without thorns" and do not prick your hands as the lote-trees of this world do. Here Allah distinguished the Gardens of the Hereafter from the gardens of this world, saying: ﴿Gardens of Eden...﴾ [18:31], meaning a lasting residence that does not end and does not cease. The gardens of this world are not like that. Suppose a man enjoys in this world houses and palaces amid the gardens and orchards which are the garden of this world; will they endure for him? The gardens of this world, however great their bliss, will either leave you, or you will leave them.

"Eden" is the name of Paradise, and there is a difference between one dwelling and another within Paradise, just as you see public gardens and private gardens. The believer in Paradise has a private dwelling in the Garden of Eden.

And the Exalted says concerning the rivers of Paradise: ﴿Beneath them rivers flow...﴾ [47:12].

In another verse He says: ﴿Beneath which rivers flow...﴾ [9:100], to give us a picture of the flowing of water. In His saying ﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾ [9:100] it indicates that the water comes to it from afar, and you might fear that someone could block it from you or dam it off in your absence; therefore He says to you: be reassured, for the water flows "from beneath them," that is, from Paradise itself, and no one can keep it from you.

In this verse it is as if the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, gives us a subtle hint that we can make dwellings on the surface of water and exploit bodies of water to build structures upon them. Take, for example, the water surfaces of the Nile, or the area from the Qanatir al-Khayriya down to Damietta: you would find large, wide spaces where, by erecting pillars in the water and using building engineering, one could construct the dwellings sufficient to house the people of these lands, while the agricultural land remains as it is, for greenery, for crops, and for the sustenance of people.

This method can also be applied in the countryside, where farmers could build their houses and animal pens in the same way over the canals and drains spread across our land, without touching the cultivated area.

The building movement has overrun Giza, Dokki and Mohandessin, which were once lands yielding every kind of crop and supplying Cairo's provisions. When they brought foreign experts to expand Cairo, they turned to the desert and founded Heliopolis, and none of them encroached upon a single span of agricultural land; rather, in their planning they set a green area for every house.

So in the verse there is a subtle indication that can resolve our housing crisis and protect our narrow cultivated area. Then the Exalted says: ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [18:31].

Someone may say: what are these gold bracelets with which men adorn themselves? These are of the ornaments and embellishments; we see it now in human ambitions for the adornment of life, where young people wear what is called the "ankle bracelet" (inseal). Likewise, gold bracelets in the Hereafter are an adornment and ornament. In another verse the Exalted says: ﴿And they will be adorned with bracelets of silver﴾ [76:21].

And again He says: ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold and pearls, and their clothing therein will be silk﴾ [35:33].

So the bracelets are of gold, or silver, or pearls. Therefore the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning this adornment in the Hereafter that it will reach as far as the ablution of the believer reaches. We note in His saying ﴿They will be adorned therein with bracelets of gold﴾ [18:31] that the adornment here is for ornament, not one of the necessities; therefore the verb is "yuhallawna" (they are adorned), i.e., others adorn them, and He did not say "yatahallawna" (they adorn themselves). Hence, when He spoke after it of clothing, which is a necessity, He said: ﴿and they will wear green garments of fine green silk and brocade﴾ [18:31].

Here He used the verb in the active voice, because the action proceeded from them themselves by their work; whereas the former adornment was by the grace of Allah, and He placed grace before work, as He says in another verse: ﴿Say: "By the grace of Allah and His mercy, let them rejoice in that"﴾ [10:58]; that is: beware of saying this is by your deeds, rather it is by the grace of Allah and His mercy.

This is because, if you look at your deeds, you will find them after the obligation you were charged with at the age of puberty, and you have lived all this time reveling in Allah's blessings and provision without being charged with anything. Therefore, however much obedience you offer to Allah, it will never repay what He has bestowed upon you.

What you do of acts of obedience is only fulfilment of the right of Allah; so if we admit you to Paradise, it is a grace from Allah upon you, because you already took your right in advance in this world. But He distributed it here, saying: ﴿and they will wear...﴾ [18:31], that is, according to what they did; whereas for adornment and embellishment He said "yuhallawna," like a man who prepares his daughter for marriage, providing her with the necessities of life and then adding to them the luxuries and ornaments of life, such as chandeliers, carpets, or the like.

Clothing is one of the necessities of life with which Allah has favoured His servants, as He says: ﴿O children of Adam, We have sent down to you clothing to cover your private parts and as adornment (rish)﴾ [7:26]. The rish is the luxuries that people take for show and enjoyment, that which exceeds the necessities. Sundus is fine thin silk, and istabraq is thick heavy silk.

The scholars have paused at this word "istabraq" and other non-Arabic words such as "qistas" (balance), which are of Persian origin, or the word "amin" which we adopt as a formula in prayer, whose origin is Yemeni or Abyssinian. They said: how does the Qur'an use such words, when it is an Arabic Qur'an?

We say: did the Qur'an introduce these words into the language of the Arabs at the time it was revealed, or did the Qur'an come while these words were already passing on people's tongues, used by them and used in mutual understanding? The Arabs knew these words and used them, and they became Arabic words that circulated on the tongues and took the course of an Arabic word.

Among the words that entered Arabic recently and have been used as an Arabic word is "bank" (bank), which is perhaps lighter in use than the word "masraf" (bank/financial institution); therefore the Academy of the Arabic Language approved it and admitted it into Arabic.

Therefore: this view could be accepted if the Qur'an had introduced these words as a first occurrence and brought them into the language when they did not exist; but the Qur'an came to address the Arabs, and since they understood these words and addressed one another with them, they had become part of their language.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿reclining therein on couches﴾ [18:31]. Reclining (al-ittika'): that a person sits on the side that comforts him; and the arā'ik (couches) are the beds that have ornamentation, like a canopy bed, for example.

﴿How excellent a reward!﴾ [18:31]: a logical statement. ﴿And how fine a resting-place!﴾ [18:31]: that is, this is what is fitting for their situation there, in contrast to what He reported about the people of the Fire: ﴿And how evil a resting-place!﴾ [18:29].

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 32:

The discourse continues with those people who wanted to turn the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) away from those who call upon their Lord morning and evening, seeking His countenance. Through this, people were divided into two groups: a group that is arrogant, greedy for its standing and authority, and a group that is weak and humble, having neither standing nor authority. But Allah, glorified is He, wills that His signs be made to reach everyone in a way that encompasses all and levels them equally.

Therefore, Allah, glorified and exalted is He, willed to set forth for us an example existing in life: among people there is the disbelieving rich man and the believing poor man, and you must reflect on the position of each of them. His, exalted is He, saying:

﴿And set forth for them the parable of two men...﴾ [18:32]

(Surat al-Kahf).

We have said: *al-darb* (striking) means that you touch one thing against another stronger than it with a force that causes it pain, and the striker must be stronger than the struck. Otherwise, if you strike with your hand something stronger than you, you have struck yourself. Among this is the saying of the poet:

"O you who strike the stone with his staff*
Did the staff strike, or did it strike the stone?"

Setting forth a *mathal* (parable, example) serves to arouse attention and awareness, moving you from one state to another. Likewise, the parable: a thing that is obscure, which you do not understand or comprehend, so Allah, glorified is He, sets forth for it an example that clarifies it and draws your attention to it. Therefore He said:

﴿And set forth for them the parable of two men...﴾ [18:32] (Surat al-Kahf). We have already explained that *amthal* (parables) are a form of Arab speech: one intends a certain meaning, then it spreads on people's tongues and becomes a well-known proverb, as we say: "The generosity of Hatim," and when you meet any generous person you call him: "O Hatim!" When Hatim became famous for generosity, that quality was attributed to him. 'Amr ibn Ma'd became famous for bravery and boldness, Iyas became famous for intelligence, and Ahnaf ibn Qays became famous for forbearance. Therefore Abu Tammam said in praise of the caliph:

"The boldness of 'Amr with the generosity of Hatim,
the forbearance of Ahnaf with the intelligence of Iyas."

Abu Tammam's opponents then wanted to belittle his words and make the caliph think less of him, so they said to him: "The caliph is above those you have described. How can you liken the caliph to these people, when in his army there are a thousand like 'Amr, and in his treasury a thousand like Hatim? How can you compare him to the uncouth Arabs?" As one of them said:

"The panegyrists liken him in valour and wealth
to one who, if he saw him, would be a lesser servant.
In his army are fifty thousand like 'Antar,
and in his treasury a thousand Hatims."

Allah inspired him to answer them, in the same metre and the same rhyme, so he said:

"Do not deny my striking for him, besides Him,
a parable, unique in generosity and valour.
For Allah has struck the lesser, for His light,
a parable from the niche and the lamp."

So the parable comes to alert people and to clarify a matter that is not understood. And the Blessed and Exalted One said:

﴿Indeed, Allah is not ashamed to strike a parable, [even] of a mosquito or what is above it...﴾ [2:26] (Surat al-Baqarah). Then the Noble Qur'an gives us many parables to clarify particular matters, as in His saying:

﴿The example of those who take protectors other than Allah is like the spider that takes a house; and indeed, the frailest of houses is the spider's house, if only they knew.﴾ [29:41] (Surat al-'Ankabut).

Likewise His saying concerning breaking a promise and failing to fulfil it:

﴿And do not be like she who unravels her thread after it has been [made] strong, into fibres...﴾ [16:92] (Surat al-Nahl).

And among it is His saying:

﴿Their example is like that of one who kindled a fire, and when it illuminated what was around him, Allah took away their light and left them in darknesses, not seeing.﴾ [2:17] (Surat al-Baqarah).

And among it is His saying, depicting the state of this world and that it is swift to pass away:

﴿And set forth for them the example of the life of this world: it is like water which We sent down from the sky, and the plants of the earth mingled with it, then it became dry stalks scattered by the winds. And Allah is ever Able over all things.﴾ [18:45] (Surat al-Kahf).

So the parable clarifies for you the hidden by means of something manifest, which everyone who hears it knows. Among this is the poet who wanted to describe the hunchback for us, portraying him with precision as though you were looking at him:

"His shoulder-blades are shortened, and his nape sinks down,
so that he seems to be about to be slapped.
As if his back had been slapped once,
and then felt it a second time, and gathered himself."

Here the Almighty says: "Strike for them, O Muhammad, a parable of the disbeliever when he becomes rich, and the poor man when he is content with faith." His saying:

﴿two men...﴾ [18:32] (Surat al-Kahf). That is: where is the locus of the parable?

﴿We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines, and surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them cultivated land.﴾ [18:32] (Surat al-Kahf).

But was this parable actually existing, and did the two men have an actual existence in history?

Yes, they were real among the Children of Israel, and they were Barakus and Yahudha. Yahudha was a believer, content, and Barakus was self-sufficient. They inherited from their father eight thousand dinars each. Barakus took his share and bought land to farm and a palace to live in, and he married, so he had two sons and attendants. As for Yahudha, he decided to give away his share in charity, and to buy with it land in Paradise and a palace in Paradise, and the pure maidens and the youths in the Garden of Eden, [preferring these] over the wife of this world, its children and its splendour. Thus Barakus was self-satisfied with what he had and was deceived by it, as the Almighty said:

﴿Indeed, man does transgress, when he sees himself self-sufficient.﴾ [96:6–7] (Surat al-'Alaq).

The beginning of loss is that blessing occupies you from the Giver of blessing, and you think that the bliss you are in is the fruit of your effort and work, and the result of your striving and skill, as Qarun said:

﴿He said: "I have only been given it on account of knowledge that is with me."﴾ [28:78] (Surat al-Qasas).

So Allah left him to his knowledge and skill; let him then guard his wealth with whatever knowledge and strength he has:

﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home.﴾ [28:81] (Surat al-Qasas). Neither his wealth nor his knowledge benefited him. Thus these are two real examples in society: a disbeliever who is arrogant, self-sufficient and exalted by his wealth, and a believer content with what Allah has apportioned to him. Consider the agricultural arrangement in His saying:

﴿We made for one of them two gardens of grapevines, and surrounded them with date palms, and placed between them cultivated land.﴾ [18:32] (Surat al-Kahf). Allah, exalted is He, has taught us to make, around orchards and gardens, a wall of date palms to serve as a windbreak that holds back air and storms. He, glorified is He, mentioned the date palms and grapes, which are among the fruits, before the crops from which comes the essential sustenance, just as He mentioned earlier the bracelets of gold, which are for adornment, before garments, which are necessities. As for His saying:

﴿two gardens...﴾ [18:32] (Surat al-Kahf). We still see this today among those who wish to safeguard the privacy of their homes; for a person has a private dwelling and has general guests, so he makes for them another dwelling so that no one may look upon his womenfolk. Therefore they call it the *salamlik* and the *haramlik*. Likewise in the saying of the Blessed and Exalted One:

﴿There was for Sheba in their dwelling a sign: two gardens on the right and on the left. "Eat of the provision of your Lord and give thanks to Him: a good land and a forgiving Lord."﴾ [34:15] (Surat Saba').

The meaning (of "أكلها"): it gave its desired produce, and "al-ukul" is what is eaten. We know that crops bring forth their fruit in succession, so that they give you something today, and something tomorrow, and something the day after, and so on.

﴿And did not fail in it in anything.﴾ [18:33] The word "tazlim" (fail, wrong) gives us a sign of doing good in this world. The earth, being inanimate matter, does not wrong; it does not withhold your right, nor waste your toil. If you give it your effort and your work, it bestows its bounty upon you: you sow in it a measure (kayla) and it gives you an ardab, and you place in it a single seed and it multiplies it into thousands.

So it is generous and bountiful, on condition that you do what is required of you of plowing, sowing, tending and watering, and the sky may also relieve you and water it for you. Therefore, when God, glorified is He, wanted to give us a parable of the multiplication of reward, He said: ﴿The parable of those who spend their wealth in the way of God is like a grain that grows seven ears, in every ear a hundred grains...﴾ [2:261]. So if the earth gives you seven hundred grains for one grain, how about the Creator of the earth? Without doubt His bounty will be greater; therefore He said after it: ﴿And God multiplies for whom He wills, and God is All-Encompassing, All-Knowing.﴾ [2:261]

So the earth does not wrong, and from the justice of the earth is that it gives you according to your toil and effort in it. And God, the Exalted, also appreciates this toil for you and thanks you for this exertion. The Prophet (ﷺ), when he saw one of the Companions whose hands had become cracked from work, said: "This is a hand that God and His Messenger love."

It is loved by God and His Messenger because it toiled and worked not merely according to its need, but beyond its need: it worked for itself and for others. For if every worker worked only according to his own need, how would the one who cannot work live?

So those with capacity and strength should work to provide for themselves and for those unable to work. Suppose you will not give anything in charity to the needy; still, you will sell what is surplus to you, and this in itself is a form of facilitating matters for people and cooperating with them.

The earth in its giving and generosity is like a mother who showers you with bounty if you show her kindness. Likewise the earth, indeed the mother by her nature may give you without return and show tenderness to you even if you are ungrateful. Likewise the earth: do you not see it bring forth for you vegetation you did not plant nor toil over? How then if you honour it with goodness? Without doubt it will increase its bounty for you.

In truth, the earth is not our mother by way of comparison only, but is our mother in reality, because we are of its dust and part of it. When a person falls ill, for example, he becomes a burden to everyone; the earth does not bear him, yet it embraces him and removes harm from him like his mother does. Likewise when he dies and becomes a corpse, from which every loving friend and every relative recoils, the earth embraces him, absorbs all that is in him, and conceals him on a day when he is most in need of concealment.

Then He, exalted, says: ﴿And We caused a river to gush forth between them.﴾ [18:33] This is because water is the origin of cultivation, so God made for the two gardens a special water that issues from them and gushes forth between them, not coming to them from outside so that anyone could block it from them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 34:

Meaning: The matter was not limited to his having two gardens containing palm trees, grapevines and crops that yield their produce. Rather, he had, in addition to that, "thamar" (fruit), i.e., other sources of wealth: gold, silver and children, because the child is the fruit of his father. Shortly after, he will say to his brother: "I am more abundant than you in wealth and mightier in men." Then this dialogue takes place between them:

﴿So he said to his companion while he was arguing with him: "I am more abundant than you in wealth and mightier in men."﴾ (Surat al-Kahf 18:34). This is evidence that what was mentioned earlier about the two gardens and the blessings in them prompted him to arrogance, and that this is the cause of his saying (to his companion). The "companion" (sahib) is the one who keeps company with you, even if you do not love him. ("Yuhawiruhu") means he debates him, such that one of them says something and the other responds, until they reach a conclusion. So what did his companion say? He said: ﴿"I am more abundant than you in wealth..."﴾ (Surat al-Kahf 18:34): he means the two gardens and the blessings in them.

﴿"...and mightier in men"﴾ (Surat al-Kahf 18:34): this is included in His saying: ﴿"And he had fruit..."﴾ (Surat al-Kahf 18:34). Thus this one was made self-sufficient by wealth and children.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 35:

We have understood that they are two gardens. So why did He say: ﴿And he entered his garden⟩ [18:35]? We say: because a person who has two gardens will not enter them both at the same time. Rather, upon entering, he will face one garden, and after that he will enter the other. And His saying: ﴿while he was wronging himself⟩ [18:35].

A person may wrong others, but how can he wrong himself? A person wrongs himself when he gives free rein to his desires, thereby depriving himself of other pleasures and forfeiting what is more lasting and greater. The wronging of a person falls upon himself, because the self (nafs) has two aspects: a self that desires, and a conscience (wijdan) that restrains by natural disposition (fitrah).

The matter, then, is a contest between these elements. For this reason they say: "The greatest enemy of a person is his own self that lies between his two sides." If you say: "How, when I and my self are one thing?" Reflect, and you will find that at the very moment you speak to yourself about something and then blame yourself for it, this is because within you there are two personalities: a natural personality, and another personality that is acquisitive and appetitive. If the appetitive self inclines or deviates, the natural self straightens it and corrects its conduct.

For this reason we have said: the divine method in all religions was that when disobedience spread among people, and there was no longer anyone who advised and guided, God sent down a messenger among them to guide and remind them. But not so with the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ), because He, glory be to Him, entrusted them with the message of their Prophet, made their guidance rest in their own hands, and brought forth from among them those who carry the banner of the call to God. Therefore they will not need another messenger, and Muhammad (ﷺ) was the Seal of the Prophets and Messengers.

It is as if He, glory be to Him, reassures us that corruption will not become universal: if disobedient ones are found within this nation, there are also among it the obedient who carry the banner of enjoining what is right and forbidding what is wrong. This is a necessary matter and a foundation upon which the Islamic society stands. Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿He said, "I do not think that this will ever perish"⟩ [18:35].

Does this mean that he wronged himself by entering? No, because it is his garden, which he enters as he wishes. Rather, what is meant by the wronging here is what passed through his mind and what he told himself upon entering. He wronged himself when the thought of arrogance through wealth and conceit in blessing occurred to him, so he said: "I do not think this blessing will perish, or this luxuriant garden will vanish or be destroyed." Indeed, a palpable reality before his eyes deceived him, such that he deemed it unlikely that all this bounty would be removed from him. Not only this, but his conceit called him to more than this.

Thus he let his arrogance run free, even though he had accepted from himself: "I do not think this will ever perish" (35). So it is not accepted from him.

"And I do not think the Hour will ever come..." (36). So, because the one who denied the Hour was shaken by the emotions of his conscience, he corrected himself, saying: "And if I am returned to my Lord..." (36). That is: in any case, if I am returned to my Lord on the Day of Resurrection, I will have something better and greater than this. It is as if he were guaranteeing that Allah, exalted is He, has prepared for him what is better than this. Let us pause to reflect on the words of this denier, who was elated by the blessing of Allah upon him and captivated by it: "And if I am returned to my Lord..." (36). Here he acknowledges that he has a Lord to whom he will return. So if he was a liar, let him at least be consistent and not contradict himself, for the arrogance, conceit and doubt about the Hour that came from him are incompatible with his saying "my Lord" and do not suit it.

And "munqalaban" means: a place of return.

Here the believing companion answers him in dialogue and debate, to make clear to him the correct view: "Do you disbelieve in He who created you from dust..." (Qur'an 18:37). That is, your earlier speech, "I am more than you in wealth and stronger in manpower" and your arrogance and denial in what you say, do you remember all of this while forgetting your beginning and origin from dust, which is the root of your creation? "Then from a drop of semen..." (Qur'an 18:37): and this is the basis of procreation. "Then He fashioned you into a man" (Qur'an 18:37): that is, complete and balanced (malu hadumak, "filled out your clothes"). And "fashioned you" (Qur'an 18:37).

Al-taswiyah (fashioning, proportioning): it is preparing a thing, preparing it in a manner suited to its task in life. We have said that a straight iron rod is "sawiy" (balanced), while the hook at its end is bent, and the bending of the hook is the very thing that makes it straight and fulfils its task, because its task is to snatch things with it; if this hook were straight, it would not perform its intended task. The hamza in "akafarta" (Qur'an 18:37) is not interrogative; rather, it is a rebuke of what his companion says, and of the disbelief and forgetfulness of the reality of his affair and the beginning of his creation that proceeded from him.

Dust is the origin of man, and it is also one of the stages of his creation, because God, exalted is He, mentioned in the creation of man once "from water," once "from dust," once "from black mud moulded" (hama'in masnun), and once "from clay like pottery" (salsal ka-al-fakhkhar).

Therefore some object to these different descriptions in the creation of man. The truth is that they are one thing with multiple transitional stages: if you add water to dust it becomes mud (tin); when you mix the mud with one another it becomes black mud moulded (hama masnun); if you leave it until it dries and hardens it becomes clay (salsal). So these are stages of one thing.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 38:

His saying: ﴿But I⦆ [38]: that is, "I" (anā), so the hamza was dropped and the nun was assimilated into the nun (idghām). "But" (lākinna) is for istidrāk (correction or contrast). The believer corrects what his companion has said: "I am not like you in what you are heading toward. If you have disbelieved in the One who created you from dust, then from a drop of semen, then fashioned you into a man, I have not disbelieved in the One who created me. My word and my belief, in which I have faith, are: ﴿He is Allah, my Lord⦆ [38]." You will notice that the disbeliever did not say "Allah is my Lord"; rather, the word "my Lord" (rabbī) came from his tongue only in the course of speech. The difference between the two statements is great, because the Lord (rabb) is the Creator who takes charge of nurture, and this is a matter about which no one doubts and to which no one objects. The doubt lies only in the God who is worshipped and obeyed (al-ilāh al-ma'būd al-muṭā'). Lordship (rubūbiyyah) is a gift, but divinity (ulūhiyyah) is a obligation (taklīf). Therefore the disbeliever acknowledged lordship and denied divinity and obligation.

Then the believer affirms his faith, saying: ﴿and I will not associate anyone with my Lord⦆ [38]. The believer was not content to make clear to his companion the disbelief he was in; rather he wished to extend his faith to others. This is the nature of the believer: to be eager for the guidance of others. Therefore, after clarifying his faith in God, the Exalted, he wanted to teach his companion how to be a believer. The faith of a believer is not complete until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself. Also, it is part of the believer's reason to try to guide the disbeliever, because the believer's conduct toward others is sound, and it is also good for the believer to correct the disbeliever's conduct through faith.

Therefore, it is better that, instead of invoking curses upon your enemy, you invoke guidance for him, because your cursing him will only increase your own misery through him.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 39:

He wants to teach him the way of faith in receiving a blessing, by returning blessings to the Bestower, for the blessing in which a person revels is not his own merit; all of it is granted by God. These gardens and orchards, how did they yield their fruit? It is the earth that God created for you, and when you ploughed it, you ploughed it with an implement of wood or iron, which is also a gift from God in which you have no part. And the strength that helped you in the work is a gift to you that can be taken from you at any time, so that you become weak and unable to do anything.

Therefore, when you look into all these matters, you find that they end at the supreme giving of God, glory be to Him. Take this chair on which you sit at ease, which is extremely elegant and skilfully crafted. From where did the craftsmen get its material? If you trace it, you will find it is a piece of wood from one of the forests, and if you asked the forest: from where do you have this wood? it would answer you: from God.

Thus the Exalted and Glorified teaches us courtesy regarding His blessing upon us, by His saying: ﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the growers?﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:63-64). This grain that you have sown in your field, did you sit beside it nurturing it and drawing it up from the earth, so that it grows with you day after day? All your work in it is to plough the land and scatter the seeds. Even the act of ploughing, God subjected the beasts for you to carry out this process, and you could not have made them submissive to this work had God not subjected them to you and tamed them for your service, as He said, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have subjected them to them, so some of them they ride and some of them they eat﴾ (Surah Ya-Sin 36:72). You were not able to subject them yourself.

Therefore, if you examine any blessing in which you have a part of work, you will find that your share in it returns to God and is granted by Him, glory be to Him. Even after the crop grows and flowers or bears fruit, you cannot be sure that a blight will not strike it or a calamity befall it and destroy it; therefore He, the Exalted, says after it: ﴿If We willed, We would make it into debris, and you would remain astonished, [saying], "Indeed, we are [burdened with] debt; rather, we are deprived."﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:65-67).

As He, the Exalted, also says: ﴿Indeed, We have tested them as We tested the people of the garden, when they swore to pick its fruit in the morning, without making exception [by saying, "If God wills"]. So there went around it a visitation from your Lord while they were asleep, and it became as if harvested [black as the night].﴾ (Surah al-Qalam 68:17-20).

Likewise in His saying: ﴿Have you considered the water that you drink? Is it you who brought it down from the clouds, or are We the producer?﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:68-69). This water that you drink, sweet and pure, do you know how it came down? Have you seen the vapour of water rising into the air, and how it gathers into clouds driven by the wind? Do you comprehend this process?

﴿If We willed, We would make it salty and bitter...﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:70), that is: intensely salty, of no benefit to you.

So when God bestows any blessing upon His servants, He reminds them of what would nullify it; it is not of their striving, and they should thank Him for it so that it remains before them and does not vanish. Otherwise, let them guard it themselves if it is the product of their own hands!

Similarly, regarding the creation of man, the Exalted and Glorified makes clear that He gives life and annuls it by death. He said: ﴿Have you considered the semen that you emit? Is it you who create it, or are We the Creator? We have decreed death among you, and We are not to be outdone﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:58-60). So if you are the creators, then preserve it and ward off death from it. He, glory be to Him, mentioned the blessing in creation and what nullifies that blessing at the root of creation. As for the creation of fire, the matter differs, for He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Have you considered the fire that you kindle? Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the producer?﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:71-72). He, glory be to Him, mentioned His power in creating fire and kindling it, and did not mention what would nullify it, nor did He say: We are able to extinguish it. Just as He mentioned the creation of man and His power to annul it by death, and the creation of the crop and His power to make it debris, and the creation of water and His power to make it bitter, but not in the case of fire, because He, glory be to Him, wants it to be kindled and blazing continuously, so that it remains a reminder for people. Therefore He concluded the verse with His saying: ﴿We have made it a reminder and a utility for the travellers﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:73).

Also, in these verses we observe a feature of the miraculous nature and precision of the Qur'anic expression, for the Speaker is the Lord who speaks of everything in a manner fitting to it. In speaking of the crop, since man has a role in it, such as ploughing, sowing and irrigating and so on, we see Him emphasise the act that nullifies this crop, saying: ﴿If We willed, We would make it into debris...﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:65), so that vanity over your work does not beset you. As for speaking of water, where man has no part in its formation, there is no need to emphasise the act as in the previous case, so He says: ﴿If We willed, We would make it bitter...﴾ (Surah al-Waqi'ah 56:70), without emphasis, because man does not claim any merit in this water that pours from the sky.

Let us return to the believer who advises his disbelieving companion and teaches him how to receive God's blessing upon him: ﴿And why, when you entered your garden, did you not say, "What God willed [has occurred]; there is no power except in God"...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:39). (Lawla) means "why not" (hal), and it is for urging and reproach. A person, when he sees something that pleases him in wealth or children, even if his own face pleases him in the mirror, should say: "What God willed; there is no power except in God."

So when you behold a blessing of God, it was incumbent upon you not to let the blessing divert you from the Bestower; you should have said: "What God willed; there is no power except in God," meaning that all this is not by my strength or my cunning, but by a grace from God. Thus you return the blessing to its Creator and Giver, and since you have returned the blessing to its Creator, you have entrusted it to Him and asked Him to safeguard it, thereby guaranteeing its continuance.

We have mentioned that our master Ja'far al-Sadiq, may God be pleased with him, was knowledgeable of the treasures of the Qur'an, and he observed the human soul and what afflicts it of fluctuations that cloud the serenity of life, such as fear, anxiety, worry, sorrow, deceit, or the allure of worldly life and human ambitions in it.

So he, may God be pleased with him, would bring forth for these ailments the remedies of the Qur'an that suit them. He would say concerning fear: "I am astonished at one who fears and does not resort to the saying of God: ﴿God is sufficient for us, and He is the best Disposer of affairs﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran 3:173)."

For I have heard that God follows it with: ﴿So they returned with favour from God and bounty, not touched by evil﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran 3:174).

And I am astonished at one who is distressed, for distress is the closing of the heart and the confusion of the mind over something whose cause is unknown. I am astonished at one who is distressed and does not resort to the saying of God: ﴿There is no deity except You; exalted are You. Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya' 21:87). For I have heard that God follows it with: ﴿So We answered him and saved him from distress...﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya' 21:88),

and not only that, but: ﴿And thus do We save the believers﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya' 21:88). It is as if it were a general prescription for every believer, and not specific to the Prophet of God, Yunus, peace be upon him. The believer afflicted with distress says: ﴿There is no deity except You...﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya' 21:87), that is: I have no refuge but You, and no shelter other than You; ﴿Indeed, I have been of the wrongdoers﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya' 21:87): he acknowledges sin and shortcoming, perhaps the sin I have committed and the wrong I have done to myself is the cause of this distress I suffer.

And I am astonished at one who is plotted against, how does he not resort to the saying of God: ﴿And I entrust my affair to God...﴾ (Surah Ghafir 40:44). For I have heard that God follows it with: ﴿So God protected him from the evils of what they plotted...﴾ (Surah Ghafir 40:45). God, blessed and exalted, is the One who will Himself take up the response to them and meet their plotting with His plotting, glory be to Him, as He said: ﴿And they plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran 3:54).

And I am astonished at one who seeks the world and its adornment, the one with worldly ambitions who yearns for its ornaments, how does he not resort to His saying: ﴿What God willed; there is no power except in God...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:39).

For I have heard that God follows it with: ﴿It may be that my Lord will give me something better than your garden...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:40). If you say it over your blessing, it is preserved and grows; and if you say it over another's blessing, God will give you something better than it. The wonderful thing is that the poor believer, who possesses none of the goods of this world, guides his disbelieving companion to the key of good that increases him in the good of this world, despite the blessings of the world in which the latter revels. The key to increasing good in this world and the permanence of blessing in it is that you say:

﴿What God willed; there is no power except in God...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:39).

The believer then continues, explaining to his companion what he reproached him with, that he is poor while he is rich, and what he exalted himself over with his wealth and children: ﴿If you see me as less than you in wealth and children﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:39).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 40:

"And 'asā (perhaps) is for hope. So if the hope is from Allah, it is certainly realized without doubt. Therefore, when you say upon seeing another's blessing: 'Mā shā' Allāh, lā quwwata illā billāh' (What Allah has willed; there is no power except through Allah), Allah will give you better than what you said it upon: 'Mā shā' Allāh, lā quwwata illā billāh.' And if you acknowledge Allah's blessing upon you and return the favour to Him, glorified is He, He will increase you, as came in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿If you are grateful, I will surely increase you﴾ (Surah Ibrahim).

So His saying: ﴿So perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 40): that is, He transfers and turns the matter of wealth and poverty. You have no power to preserve this blessing, just as you have no power to bring it about from the beginning. Therefore: it is possible that my Lord gives me a blessing like your blessing, while your blessing remains as it is. But it is the will of Allah, exalted is He, to turn your blessing and remove it: ﴿and He will send upon it a reckoning from the sky﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 40). This blessing in which you take pride, and boast of its splendour, and exalt yourself over the creatures of Allah, Allah may send upon it a ḥusbān (reckoning).

Ḥusbān (a technical term meaning a precise calculated measure): the thing that is reckoned and determined with exactness and computation, as came in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The sun and the moon run by a reckoning﴾ (Surah al-Rahman, 5). The Creator, glorified and exalted is He, made the sun and the moon for knowing the time: ﴿that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾ (Surah Yunus, 5). We do not know from these the number of years and the reckoning except if they themselves are regulated by a precise order that does not fail, just as a clock: you cannot know the time by it and regulate it except if it is itself regulated. A thing cannot be a reckoning for something else unless it is itself founded upon reckoning.

Ḥasiba ḥusbānan is like ghafara ghufrānan (both are verbal nouns from the same root pattern). Allah sent upon this garden, in which its owner was deceived, a calculated and determined thunderbolt, proportioned to the size of this garden, not exceeding it to anything else, so that he would not say: "It is a general cosmic sign that struck me as it struck others." No. It is a specific thunderbolt, reckoned for this garden and not for others.

Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿and it becomes barren ground, slippery﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 40). That is: this garden, flourishing with crops and fruits, full of palm trees and grapevines, after the thunderbolt struck it, became ṣaʿīd, that is, barren land covered with dust. From this is His saying concerning tayammum: ﴿then seek pure ṣaʿīd (earth)﴾ (Surah al-Nisa', 43). Not only this, but: ﴿ṣaʿīdan zalqā (slippery ground)﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 40), that is, moistened dust on which feet slip, so that it is fit for nothing, not even walking upon it."

(ghawran): that is, sunk deep into the earth. If you say: it is possible that the water has sunk, and we could bring it out by means of machines, for example, so he cuts off his hope in any stratagem he may think of: ﴿So you will not be able to find for it a way﴾ [18:41]. That is, you will not reach it by any means of yours. Similar is His saying, in another verse: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, then who could bring you flowing water?﴾ [67:30]. Note that this speech from the believer to his disbelieving companion is merely a hope with which he addresses him: ﴿Perhaps my Lord will give me something better than your garden﴾ [18:40]. It is a hope that has not yet occurred, and has not reached the realm of the decrees of destiny.

Thus hope passed into execution, as though God had responded to the believing man and had not belied his expectation: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:42). Uhiṭa (encompassed): as though He placed around the fruit a wall that surrounds it, so that it has no outlet, as He said in another verse: ﴿and they thought that they were encompassed﴾ (Surah Yunus 10:22). And observe that He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And his fruit was encompassed﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:42), and did not say, for example, "his crops were encompassed" or "his palm trees." This is because encompassment may befall a thing and then it bears fruit afterwards, but here the encompassment fell upon the fruit itself, which is near to picking and near to being reached, and thus the calamity in it is greater. The fruit is the goal and the final yield of the crop. Then the Truth, glorified is He, depicts the remorse and regret of the owner of the garden over it: ﴿So he began to turn his palms over for what he had spent upon it﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:42). That is: he strikes one palm against the other, as a person does when a matter befalls him that he did not expect, so he stands dumbfounded, not knowing what to say, striking palm against palm, and does not speak until he recovers from the terror and astonishment of this surprise. And for what does he turn his palms? He turns his palms in regret over what he spent upon it. ﴿While it lay in ruins upon its trellises﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:42). Khawiyah (in ruins): that is, wrecked, bare and barren, as He, glorified is He, said in another verse: ﴿Or like the one who passed by a town which was in ruins upon its trellises﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:259).

It is well known that trellises are above, so when the thunderbolt descended upon it from the sky, it demolished its trellises and turned its upper part into its lower part, so the trellis fell first, and then the walls collapsed upon it. And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And he said, "Oh, I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:42). After the astonishment had struck him dumb from speech, and he began striking palm against palm, he recovered from his astonishment and burst forth with this immediate verbal outcry: ﴿"Oh, I wish I had not associated anyone with my Lord"﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:42). He wishes that he had not associated anyone with God, because the partners he had taken besides God did not benefit him.

He had no helpers or supporters to ward off what had befallen him or to prevent the ruin that had struck his garden. (Literally: "There was no group of helpers and supporters for him who would repel this which had come upon him, and prevent the destruction that had fallen upon his garden.")

﴿And he was not one who could help himself⁠﴾ [18:43]: that is, it was not fitting for him to be able to defend himself, nor was it permissible for him to do so. Why?

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on surah 18, verse 44:

Hunalika (هنالك): that is, at that time and in that condition, the moment when the thunderbolt descended from the sky, struck the garden, and left it flattened upon its trellises. There, he remembered the Bestower and wished he had not associated anyone with God. So His saying "hunalika" means: at that precise moment, the peak moment, the peak of distress and turmoil.

Hunalika has come in the Qur'an in connection with a wondrous matter that calls to an even more wondrous one. Among these is the story of our master Zakariyya, peace be upon him, when he entered upon Maryam and found provisions with her. ﴿He said: "O Maryam, from where is this for you?" She said: "It is from God. Indeed, God provides for whom He wills without account."﴾ (Surat Al 'Imran) Zakariyya, peace be upon him, was the one responsible for her, who would bring her food and drink. When he saw with her kinds of food he had not brought, he asked her where they came from. She said: "It is from God. Indeed, God provides for whom He wills without account." This statement made Zakariyya hopeful of God's bounty, and he wished to take the means, so he prayed to God to grant him a child, although his wife was barren. Then God, exalted is He, said:

﴿There Zakariyya called upon his Lord.﴾ (Surat Al 'Imran) Al-wilaya (الولاية): that you have a guardian (waliy) who supports you. The waliy is the one who stands close to you and defends you in times of hardship. In another reading, "hunaka al-wilaya" with a kasra on the waw, meaning sovereignty (al-mulk), as in His saying: ﴿"To whom belongs sovereignty today? To God, the One, the Subduer."﴾ (Surat Ghafir)

And His saying: ﴿He is better in reward﴾ (Surat al-Kahf): because He will recompense righteous deeds with a reward better than this world and all that is in it. ﴿And better in outcome﴾ (Surat al-Kahf): that is, better in final outcome, with good provision in the Garden of Eternity.

Thus God has set forth for us an example, and clarified for us the end of the disbelieving rich man and the believing poor man, and shown us that a person must not be deceived by blessings nor be deluded by luxury, because it is a gift from God. So keep the Bestower, the Benefactor, glorified is He, always in your mind, so that He preserves your blessing for you; otherwise you would be like this ingrate who became arrogant and deluded by God's blessing, and his outcome was as you have seen.

This is an example concerning a particular matter related to one individual responsible for his actions, but if you look at it you will find it encompasses the whole world; it is a miniature image of the state of the worldly life. For this reason, the Truth, glorified is He, moved from the particular example to the general one.

Almighty God, in this verse, clarifies for us the unknown by means of what is known to us. The people of rhetoric (ahl al-balaghah) say: in this verse there is a tashbih tamthil (an extended comparison, or analogy by representation), because He, glory be to Him, likened the state of the worldly life in its brevity and swift passing to water that descends from the sky, whereby the earth is watered and brings forth various kinds of crops and fruits; but soon this vegetation withers and becomes dry, crumbled stubble, which the wind carries away.

This, as they say, is an image drawn from multiple elements (muntaza'ah min muta'addid). That is, the point of resemblance (wajh al-shabah) in it is not one thing but several things. If the comparison is composed of many things, it is called a mathal (a parable). If it is the comparison of a single thing with a single thing, they call it a mithl, and we say: "this is the like (mithl) of that." Therefore the Exalted said: ﴿So do not strike forth examples for Allah﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 74), because for Allah is the highest likeness (al-mathal al-a'la).

Thus the world appears beautiful, flowering, fruitful, sweet and fresh, and suddenly you find nothing in your hands of it. Therefore the Qur'an named it dunya (the "nearer" or "lowly" life), a name that suggests lowliness; otherwise, what description less than this could be applied to it? Let us know that what stands in contrast to it is the higher life.

It is as if Almighty God were saying to His Messenger (ﷺ): just as you struck for them the parable of the two men and what their affair came to, strike for them the parable of the life of this world, that it turns over with its people and changes them, and strike for them a parable of the world from the reality of the world itself. The meaning of ﴿so there mingled with it the vegetation of the earth﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 45): that is, the vegetation of the earth became intermingled by means of it, some of it entering into other parts, its branches and sprigs interlacing. This is the image of vegetation in fertile land; as for land that is salty and not fertile, it produces plants singly, a stalk here and a stalk there.

But did the plant remain in the state of its greenness and freshness? No, rather it soon dried out, broke, and became stubble which the wind scatters and blows away. This is a parable of the world when it takes its adornment and beautifies itself, as He said: ﴿until, when the earth takes its adornment and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day...﴾ (Surah Yunus, 24).

Then He said: ﴿And Allah is ever over all things Omnipotent﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 45), because He, glory be to Him, is always capable of turning a thing into its opposite, as He said: ﴿And indeed, We are able to take it away﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun, 18). He, glory be to Him, has power over bringing into existence and has power over annihilation, so the attribute of power never leaves Him at all: He gives life and causes death, exalts and abases, withholds and extends, harms and benefits... And since the preceding discussion was about the owner of the garden who was deceived by his wealth and children, it was fitting to speak of wealth and children.

Such are the essential elements of the trial of people in this world: wealth and children. But why is wealth mentioned first? Is it more precious to people than children? We say: Allah, glorified is He, placed wealth before children, not because it is more honored or more precious, but because wealth is general in its addressees, unlike children. Every person has wealth, however little it may be, whereas children are a particular privilege, and some people are deprived of them.

Moreover, children do not come except through wealth, because a person needs marriage and maintenance in order to beget and have offspring. Thus every individual has wealth, but not every individual has children. The ruling here is a general matter, namely: ﴿Wealth and children are the adornment of the life of this world...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:46). The word (adornment) means that they are not among the necessities of life; rather, they are merely a form and an embellishment. For the believer who is content with what Allah has apportioned to him lives his life happily without wealth and without children, because a person may be made miserable by his wealth or miserable by his child, to the extent that he wishes he had died before being given this wealth or this child.

The matter of begetting children has become a knotted problem for many people. You see a man sorrowful and grieved because he wants a child so that he may have strength and honor, and perhaps the child is born and he sees humiliation at his hands. How many problems are stirred up in homes because the wife does not bear children!

If people were certain that bringing into existence is a blessing from Allah, and that withholding is also a blessing from Allah, everyone would be at ease. Have we not read the saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿To Allah belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth. He creates what He wills. He bestows females upon whom He wills, and He bestows males upon whom He wills. Or He pairs them, males and females, and He makes whom He wills barren. Indeed, He is Knowing and Competent﴾ (Surah ash-Shura 42:49-50)?

Thus, barrenness in itself is a blessing and a gift from Allah. If a person accepts it from his Lord, Allah will compensate him for his barrenness by making all the children his children; they look to him and treat him as a father to them, so he tastes through them the pleasure of children without having toiled in raising any of them or bearing the worry of any of them.

Likewise, the one who is distressed because Allah has granted him daughters rather than sons, and who becomes like the one of whom Allah said: ﴿When one of them is given good tidings of a female, his face darkens, and he suppresses grief﴾ (Surah an-Nahl 16:58): he wants a son so that he may have strength and honor. He forgets that the honor of the believer is in Allah, not in other than Him. We say: By Allah, if a daughter were received with joy and contentment as a gift from Allah, she would be a cause for a husband to come to you who is more dutiful to you than your son, and then she herself may bring you a child who is dearer to you than your son. Thus: wealth and children are among the adornments of life and its embellishments, and they are not among the necessities.

Whatever exceeds that is part of the adornment. So a person can live without wealth or children, living by values that bring him good, and a contentment that makes him pleased with his Creator, exalted is He. Then He, exalted is He, says: ﴿But the enduring good deeds are better with your Lord in reward and better in hope﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:46). Because wealth and children will not enter the grave with you, nor will they protect you from punishment; only the enduring good deeds will benefit you.

When the Prophet (ﷺ) was given a sheep as a gift, Lady ʿĀʾishah (may Allah be pleased with her) knew that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved the shoulder of the sheep, because it is tender, light meat. So she kept the shoulder for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and gave the rest in charity. When he (ﷺ) came, he said: "What did you do with the sheep?" She said: "It has all gone except its shoulder." The Prophet (ﷺ) smiled and said: "Rather, all of it has remained except its shoulder."

In another hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Does the son of Adam have any of his wealth except what he eats and finishes, or what he wears and wears out, or what he gives in charity and so preserves?" This is the meaning of: ﴿But the enduring good deeds are better...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:46).

The question that now comes to mind: if wealth and children are not a necessity of life, then what are the necessities of life?
