The necessities of life are everything that makes this world a field for the Hereafter, and a means to an everlasting, enduring, pleasant, and happy life, in which you never finish with bliss and leave it, nor does bliss finish with you and leave you. It is the bliss of Paradise.

The necessities, then, are religion, the method of Allah, and the values that organize the movement of life according to what Allah willed in creating life. As for the meaning of: ﴿And the enduring...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:46): since He said "the enduring," this means that what precedes it was not among the enduring things, but is perishable with the passing of this world. Then He described them as "the good ones" to distinguish them from the "enduring evil deeds," by which people abide in the Fire.

﴿But the enduring good deeds are better...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:46): better with whom? Because every thing attributed to something takes on the strength of what it is attributed to. Your good is not the same as the good of one who is richer than you, nor the good of the ruler. So what about the good with Allah?

﴿...better with your Lord in reward and better in hope﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:46): "hope" (amal) is what a person aspires to, of what his condition has not yet reached. If he has some good, he aspires to something higher than it. The highest hope is with Allah, blessed and exalted. All of this shows us that this world is passing, and that we are going to a lasting day. Therefore, after "the enduring good deeds," the Truth, glorified is He, added what suits them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 47:

That is: remember well the Day when We set the mountains in motion and this world comes to an end, and do the enduring good deeds, for We shall set in motion the mountains that you see as fixed and firm, which generations inherit in their size and mass, their strength and solidity, and which remain in their state.

The meaning of setting the mountains in motion is removing them from their places, as He said in another verse: ﴿And the mountains will be set in motion, becoming a mirage﴾ (Surah An-Naba', 20), and He said in another verse: ﴿And when the mountains are set in motion﴾ (Surah At-Takwir, 3), and He said: ﴿On the Day when the sky will be like molten brass, and the mountains will be like wool, fluffed up﴾ (Surah Al-Ma'arij, 8-9).

We note that the Almighty mentioned the strongest and most stable manifestation in worldly life, for otherwise on earth there are other strong and stable things, such as buildings, skyscrapers, great and massive long-lived trees, and much more. If the Almighty is going to crush these mountains and remove them from their places, then whatever else is on the face of the earth is bound to perish all the more.

Then He, glorified be He, says: ﴿And you will see the earth laid bare﴾ (Surah Al-Kahf, 47). The earth (al-ard): everything that carries you of this expanse on which we live; and everything that rises above you and shades you is sky (sama'). The meaning of (bariza, laid bare): al-baraz is open space, that is: you will see the earth as open space, empty of what was on it of mountains, buildings and trees, even the sea that covers a large part of the earth.

All these forms have gone and have no existence, so it is as if the earth has come out after having been hidden: some of it under mountains, some under trees, some under buildings, and some under water, and it has become a wide open space with no landmark for anything in it.

From this is what we call al-mubarza (the duel/confrontation) among us: one sees a young man telling the other, "Come out to me outside" (ut'la' li bara), that is, to an empty place where he finds nothing to shelter behind, or a wall for example to lean on. And "Fulan barraza Fulanan" means he wrestled with him.

﴿And We shall gather them﴾ (Surah Al-Kahf, 47): that is, We shall assemble them for the Day of Reckoning, because they departed from the world in stages since Adam, peace be upon him, and death reaps souls, and the day has come when these will be gathered.

﴿And We shall leave none of them behind﴾ (Surah Al-Kahf, 47): that is, We shall not leave any one of them; all are presented before Allah. The word (nughadir, leave behind) and the root (gh-d-r) all carry the meaning of leaving, for treachery (al-ghadr), for example, is leaving fidelity and betraying a trust; even a ghadir, which is a small stream of water, is so called because when rain falls on the earth it goes away and leaves a little in the hollows.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 48:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:48). Al-'Ard (presentation): that the one presenting (al-'arid) confronts the one presented (al-ma'rud) in an orderly confrontation that shows every state of it, just as a commander reviews the troops in a military parade, for example, so that he sees each one of his soldiers. (Saffan): that is, in orderly rows. Even the angels come in rows, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ (Surah al-Fajr 89:22). That is: it is an organized process in which no one can hide, none of them will have any escape, and they are rows so interlocked that no row hides the row that follows it; everyone is clearly visible in every one of their conditions.

And in the hadith narrated from Mu'adh ibn Jabal, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) told us, saying: 'Allah will gather the creation, then He will call out: O My servants, bring forth your proofs and make your answers easy, for you are gathered, you will be reckoned, and you will be questioned. O My angels, set My servants in rows on the tips of the toes of their feet for the reckoning.'"

You can imagine the suffering and pain that one who stands on the tips of his toes endures, because the weight of the body is distributed over the two feet when standing, over the buttocks when sitting, and over the whole body when lying down; thus the weight of the body lightens according to the state one is in. If the whole weight is concentrated on the tips of the toes, then it is undoubtedly a painful and arduous position, difficult for people to bear, to the point that they wish to be dismissed, even if to the Fire. Then He, the Exalted, says: ﴿Indeed you have come to Us just as We created you the first time﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:48). That is: in the state in which you descended from your mother's womb, naked, possessing nothing, not even anything to cover your private parts. This meaning has been detailed in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you have certainly come to Us alone, just as We created you the first time, and you have left behind what We had bestowed upon you, and We do not see with you your intercessors whom you claimed were partners [in Allah]. Relations between you have been severed, and lost from you is what you used to claim﴾ (Surah al-An'am 6:94).

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿But you claimed that We would not appoint for you an appointment﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:48). The address here is directed to the disbelievers who denied resurrection and reckoning. (Za'amtum): and al-za'm (claim) is the mount of falsehood.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 18, verse 49:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Book will be placed﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:49): That is, the angels will place it, by the command of Allah, exalted is He, and they will give each person his book. Thus there are multiple scenes. Whoever takes his book in his right hand rejoices and says: ﴿Here, read my book!﴾ (Surah al-Haqqah 69:19). He displays it to people, proud of what is in it, because it is a noble book with nothing in it to cause shame. Therefore he boasts of it and invites people to read it, like the student who has obtained high marks, who flies with them to display them and make them known.

This is in contrast to the one who is given his book in his left hand, for he says: ﴿Oh, I wish I had not been given my book, and had not known what my account is! Oh, I wish it had been the end [of me]! My wealth has not availed me. My authority has gone from me﴾ (Surah al-Haqqah 69:25-29). It is disgrace, humiliation and regret over a shameful record.

﴿Then you will see the criminals fearful of what is in it﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:49): That is, afraid and trembling. The Exalted Truth portrays for us this state of fear so that He may alarm His servants, warn them, and magnify the punishment for them, while they are still in a time of remedy and correction of conduct. This is from the mercy of Allah, exalted is He, toward His servants.

Their first state is ishfaq (apprehension), which is the process of the heart sinking and trembling. Then comes the utterance of speech: ﴿And they say, "Oh woe to us!"﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:49). Ya (يا) is a particle of calling, as if they are saying: "O our regret! O our destruction! This is your time, so come forth!" From this is His saying, exalted is He, concerning the story of the two sons of Adam, peace be upon him, when Qabil killed Habil, and that was the first incident of killing and the first death among the descendants of Adam. Therefore Allah sent to him a raven to teach him how to bury his brother, and he said: ﴿Oh woe to me! Am I unable to be like this raven and conceal the corpse of my brother?﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:31).

﴿Oh woe to me!﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah 5:31): O my destruction, as one who laments over what he has come to be in, and that the raven is more intelligent than him and more experienced than him. So that we do not wrong these creatures by saying that they are beasts that do not understand, while the truth is: would that we were like them. His saying, exalted is He: ﴿What is this Book that leaves neither a small thing nor a great thing but has enumerated it?﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:49): That is, it does not leave any small or great deed without counting and reckoning it.

﴿And they will find what they did present﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:49): So everything they did is recorded and inscribed in their books.

﴿And your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:49): Because He, exalted is He, is just; He does not hold them accountable except for what they did.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 50:

The story of the angels' prostration to Adam, peace be upon him, is repeated many times in the Noble Qur'an, and each time the verses give us a particular snapshot. In this verse, the Truthful (al-Haqq), glory be to Him, says to us: You must remember well the enmity of Iblis toward your father Adam, and remember well that he took a covenant upon himself before God, exalted is He, that he would lead you all astray. So you should have been alert to this enmity, and whenever he tells you something, remember his enmity toward you.

When al-Haqq, glory be to Him and exalted is He, warns us about Iblis, He is nurturing in us the immunity (al-manaah) with which we resist him. Immunity is that you bring in, in the form of a dormant germ, something that would harm you in the future, when it surprises you, and you place it in the body. This is the vaccination (al-tatkeem) that trains the body to repel the disease and overcome it if it strikes.

Likewise, al-Haqq, glory be to Him, gives us immunity against Iblis, and reminds us of what he did to our father Adam, and of his arrogance in refusing to prostrate to him. And we should always remember his saying: ﴿Have You seen this one whom You have honored above me? If You delay me until the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize his descendants, except for a few﴾ (Surah al-Isra' 17:62). So be alert, for as long as we shall see the mountains moved, the earth leveled, and every person's book laid open. Beware lest you stand in a dreadful position on the Day of Resurrection, and then be startled by a book that leaves nothing small or great unrecorded. Here I am reminding you now, in a time of ease and opportunity to make amends, so endeavour to repent to God and to set right what lies between you and your Lord.

The command here came to the angels: ﴿And when We said to the angels...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:50), because they are the noblest of creatures, for they do not disobey God in what He commands them, and they do what they are commanded. When God, exalted is He, commands the angels who have these attributes to prostrate to Adam, this means submission, and that this is the vicegerent (khalifah) whom I command you to be in service to. Therefore He named them "those who arrange affairs" (al-mudabbirat amran), and the Exalted said of them: ﴿For him are successive angels before and behind him, who guard him by the command of God﴾ (Surah al-Ra'd 13:11). So it is as if the task of these angels is to be with mankind and in their service.

If al-Haqq, glory be to Him, has mobilized these angels, who are the noblest of creatures, to serve man, and commanded them to prostrate to him as a declaration of submission to man, then it is all the more fitting that the whole cosmos, with its heavens and its earth, should submit to him and be at his service. He mentioned only the noblest of creatures so that the ruling would extend to those beneath them.

We have said that scholars have differed greatly over the nature of Iblis: is he of the jinn or of the angels? This verse has cut off and settled this dispute, for the Exalted said: ﴿Except Iblis; he was of the jinn...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:50).

Since the Qur'an has come with an explicit text clarifying his kind, no one may say that he is of the angels. And since he was of the jinn, who are a kind endowed with choice in doing or not doing, he chose not to do: ﴿So he defied the command of his Lord...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:50), that is, he returned to his origin and departed from the command. As for His saying: ﴿Will you then take him and his offspring as allies instead of Me, while they are enemies to you?...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:50): this is a strange matter. How, after what he has done, will you make him an ally instead of God, who created you and provided for you? He is more deserving of this allegiance. And His saying: ﴿and his offspring...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:50) indicates the procreation of Iblis, and that he has children, and that they intermarry. One may also say that "his offspring" means everyone who follows his way in misguidance and seduction, even if he be of mankind, as the Exalted said: ﴿And thus We have appointed for every prophet an enemy: devils of mankind and of the jinn, inspiring one another with decorated speech in deception﴾ (Surah al-An'am 6:112).

﴿Evil is the exchange for the wrongdoers﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:50): that is, how evil is the substitute, that you take as an ally Iblis, who refused and was arrogant to prostrate to your father, and abandon the allegiance of God, who commanded the angels to prostrate to your father.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 51:

Indeed, this Satan whom you have taken as a patron besides Allah, to whom you have given precedence and whom you have listened to, did not witness the creation of the heavens and the earth, not even as mere observers. They were not present for it, because the creation of the heavens and the earth came before their creation. Likewise, they did not witness the creation of themselves, for at the hour of their creation they did not exist. They did not witness any of that, so that they could inform you.

﴿Nor did I take the misguiders as helpers (ʿadud).﴾ (Surat al-Kahf) : That is, as assistants, aides and supporters. So I did not make them witness the creation, and they did not help me in it.

The ʿadud (ʿaḍud, "upper arm" or "support") is the strength that aids you and supports you, and it is derived from the upper arm of a human being, with which he performs most of his works by hand. When he works with his hand, a group of limbs move within it: gripping, extending, and turning right, left, up and down. All these movements require an organiser or a motor, which is the upper arm. In the movement of the hand and the precision with which it performs its task, there are great signs that indicate the precision of the craftsmanship.

When humans have made machines resembling the human arm and hand from modern equipment, you find, for example, the bulldozer driver performing several movements in order to move this machine. As for you, you move your hand as you wish without knowing what happens. How is this movement accomplished for you merely by thinking about it, without effort or arrangement from you?

All your parts are subjected to your will: if you wish to stand, for instance, you stand immediately. Therefore, beware of thinking that you are a mechanical creation. Rather, you are a divine craftsmanship, far removed from the mechanics of machines, as evidenced by the fact that if the All-Creator, glorified is He, wishes to stop a part of you, He commands the brain to cut its connection to it, and total paralysis occurs, and you cannot repel it or repair it.

Among this also is the words of Allah Almighty in the story of Musa: ﴿We will strengthen your arm through your brother...﴾ (Surat al-Qasas).

That is: We will strengthen you and give you support and help.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 52:

That is: "Recall, O Muhammad, and let your community also recall this Day: ﴿And [mention] the Day He will say, 'Call My partners whom you claimed.'﴾" (Surat al-Kahf). The Truth, glorified is He, says to the disbelievers: "Call upon My partners whom you took besides Me." "And you claimed" means: you lied in your claim that they are gods. ﴿So they will call them, but they will not respond to them.﴾ (Surat al-Kahf).

This is what their shamelessness, their audacity and their bad manners toward the Truth, glorified is He, amounted to. It was incumbent upon them to be ashamed before Allah, to return to the Truth, and to acknowledge what they had denied; but they persisted. ﴿So they will call them...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf). It is also permissible that among the partners there are people who are not accountable, and people who are above accountability. For example, among them are those whom they said were Jesus, and among them those whom they said was 'Uzayr (Ezra), and this is false. Did they respond to them?

Among them are those who took other gods, such as the sun, the moon, idols and others. Among them are those who worshipped people like themselves and obeyed them, and these were present with them. It is possible that they called upon them and summoned them: "Come, argue on our behalf, and bring us out of what we are in. We worshipped you and were obedient to your command," just as Allah the Exalted said about them: ﴿We only worship them so that they may bring us nearer to Allah in position.﴾ (Surat az-Zumar). But how could they attain what they desire? For the ties between them have been severed, and their argument has been cut off.

﴿So they will not respond to them.﴾ (Surat al-Kahf). Then the Truth, glorified is He, placed between the caller and the called a deep valley: ﴿And We will make between them a barrier of destruction.﴾ (Surat al-Kahf). The "mawbiq" is the place where destruction occurs, and it is a valley among the valleys of Hell in which they will all be destroyed. Or: between the caller and the called there is a place of ruin, so the caller cannot seek refuge with the called, nor can the called come to the aid of the caller and help him, because between them is a wellspring of destruction. From this is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If He wills, He stills the wind, so they remain motionless upon its surface. Indeed in that are signs for everyone patient and grateful. Or He wrecks them for what they have earned, and pardons much.﴾ (Surat ash-Shura). That is: He destroys them. And it is strange that this should be the first obedience they render to Allah, the Exalted: when He said to them, ﴿"Call My partners"﴾ (Surat al-Kahf), they responded to this command, although they had not obeyed the other commands.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 53:

ra'a (رأى): al-ru'ya (الرؤية) is the falling of sight upon the thing seen. The seeing here is by those who are to be punished in the Fire. It may also be seeing by the Fire that will punish them, because it sees them, awaits them and calls out to them, as the Exalted said: ﴿On the Day We say to Hell, "Are you filled?" and it says, "Are there any more?"﴾ (Surah Qaf, 50:30). That is: "Here I am, waiting for them and ready to meet them."

al-mujrimun (والمجرمون): those who committed crimes, and at their head is disbelief in Allah. So the seeing here is mutual: the one punished and the punisher each see the other and recognise one another. And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they will be certain that they are about to fall into it...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 18:53).

Here, al-zann (الظن, "supposition") is intended to mean certainty. That is: they were certain that they would fall into it, as in the words of the Truthful, glory be to Him: ﴿Those who are certain that they will meet their Lord...﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:46), that is, those who are certain. ﴿And they will find no escape from it﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 18:53). That is: while there is a barrier (mawbiq) between them, they also find no refuge (mafarr) to flee to, no shelter (malja') to seek, and no place (masraf) to turn to away from the Fire. The mawbiq exists, and the masraf is absent.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 18, verse 54

We have previously discussed the notion of tasrif al-ayat (the variation of the verses), and we said that tasrif means transforming a thing into many different things, just as God turns the winds, for example, so that they do not come from one direction alone, but come once from here and once from there. Likewise, God has varied the parables. That is, He has brought them in many different states and diverse forms.

The Truth, glory be to Him, strikes parables as if He is knocking with them on people's ears regarding a matter that may be hidden from them, so He represents it by a matter that is clear and perceptible to them, so that they may understand it with precise understanding.

Since the Truth, glory be to Him, has varied in this Qur'an from every parable, there is no excuse for one who does not understand. The Qur'an has come in many aspects so that people may learn according to the differences of their understandings and their talents. Thus you see the unlettered man hear it and take from it according to his understanding, and the semi-educated man hear it and take from it according to his culture, and the great scholar take from it according to his knowledge and find in it his desire. Moreover, the specialist in any field of knowledge finds in the Book of God the most subtle details, because the Truth, glory be to Him, has made everything clear in it.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿And man is ever most contentious (jadalan)﴾ [al-Kahf 18:54]. That is: he is much given to dispute and to contention over opinions. Jadal (disputation) is debate, and the attempt by each party to establish the truth of its position and its speech. Disputation is either in falsehood, to establish the proofs of desires and to employ evasion so as to justify your position even if it is wrong, and this is the blameworthy disputation founded on desires. Or it is in truth, and this is constructive disputation which aims to reach the reality, and this is far removed from partiality to whim or aims.

When the Noble Qur'an spoke of disputation, the Exalted said: ﴿And do not dispute with the People of the Book except in a manner that is best﴾ [al-'Ankabut 29:46], and He said: ﴿And argue with them in a manner that is best﴾ [al-Nahl 16:125].

The Prophet (ﷺ), when he passed by 'Ali and Fatimah (may Allah be pleased with them both) to wake them for the Fajr prayer, knocked on their door again and again, and it appears that they were deeply asleep. The Prophet (ﷺ) called out to them: "Will you not pray?" 'Ali replied: "O Messenger of Allah, our souls are in the hand of Allah; if He wills to release them, He releases them, and if He wills to hold them, He holds them." The Prophet (ﷺ) laughed and said: ﴿And man is ever most contentious﴾ [al-Kahf 18:54].

Because man has many desires and diverse thoughts, and he seeks to prove the soundness of his desires and thoughts by argument, so he contends with the truth, equivocates, and evades. If you examine his opinion carefully, you will find that he has a desire he strives for and inclines to achieve. You see this clearly when you choose one of the roads for you and your companion to take, for example, because it is the easiest and nearest; then he suggests to you another road and tries to persuade you of it by every means, while the reality is that he has an aim in himself and a desire he wants to reach.

What prevented them from believing when the Qur'an had come down to them, and We had varied in it the signs and the parables, after it came to them in agreement with every circumstance?

In another verse, the Truthful (al-Haqq) subhanahu explained the reason for their turning away from faith, and He said, Exalted is He:

﴿And We have certainly varied for the people in this Qur'an from every example, but most of the people refused except disbelief. And they said, "We will not believe you until you cause to gush forth for us from the earth a spring, Or you have a garden of palm trees and grapevines and cause rivers to burst forth within it in force, Or you cause the sky to fall upon us in fragments as you have claimed, or you bring Allah and the angels before us in union, Or you have a house of gold, or you ascend into the sky. And we will not believe in your ascension until you bring down to us a book we can read."﴾ (Surat al-Isra')

All these obstinate demands and this stubbornness are what came between them and belief in Allah. When the Truthful, exalted is He, brings a sign that the people asked for and they then do not believe in it, He destroys them. Therefore He said after it:

﴿Except that there come to them the way of the former peoples...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 55)

That is the sign that awaits them: that the sanction of Allah come upon them in destroying those who denied the messengers.

Before Islam, it was the sky that intervened to support the creed, so it would crush their towns and dwellings upon them. The Messenger's duty was only the call and the delivery, and it was not part of his mission to call people to war and jihad in the way of spreading his call. But the nation of Muhammad (ﷺ) was entrusted with bearing the sword to discipline those who go out of obedience to Allah. And His saying, Exalted is He:

﴿Or that they seek forgiveness from their Lord...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 55): that is, for what passed of wrangling, obstinacy, and arrogance in refusing to accept the truth.

﴿Except that there come to them the way of the former peoples...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 55): that is, the destruction of the deniers.

﴿Or that the punishment come to them face to face﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 55): that is, confronting them and visible before them. Or "qubulan" is the plural of "qabil," meaning various kinds of punishment, as He said, Exalted is He:

﴿And indeed, for those who have wronged there is a punishment besides that...﴾ (Surat al-Tur, 47): that is, for them there is a punishment other than the Fire, so their kinds of punishment are many.

Then the Truthful, exalted is He, consoles His Messenger (ﷺ) so that he does not heed the deeds of the disbelievers and does not destroy himself with grief over their turning away.

We have said that argument may be for the truth, and it may be for falsehood, as those who disbelieve do here: they dispute with falsehood and employ every trick to refute the truth, that is, to render it inoperative and remove it. ﴿And they took My signs and what they were warned of as a mockery﴾ [18:56].

That is: the cosmic signs that came to confirm the messengers, and likewise the signs of the Qur'an and the signs of the legal rulings, they took as objects of ridicule and mockery, and they paid no heed to the warning contained in them.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 57:

﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord, but turns away from them and forgets what his hands have sent forward?﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): The statement has come in the form of a question in order to emphasise the speech. It is as if your companion claims that you did not visit him and did not do him a favour. It is possible for you to say to him: "I did such-and-such for you," as a plain statement from you, and a plain statement may be true or may be false.

But if the matter is presented in the form of a question, and you say to him: "Did I not do such-and-such for you?", you will draw from him an acknowledgement of that, and you establish the proof against him from his own words. You never question an opponent except while you are confident that his answer will be only what you wish. In this way, the Exalted One brought the statement into the form of a question: ﴿And who is more unjust than one who is reminded of the signs of his Lord...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf), and He left the answer for us to say: no one is more unjust than one who does that. Acknowledgement is the master of proofs. His saying ﴿...but turns away from them...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) means: he abandons them.

﴿...and forgets what his hands have sent forward﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): he forgets the evil deeds. It was obligatory for him to pay attention to these signs and believe in them, so that God would turn to him in mercy through his faith and change his evil deeds into good deeds. Then the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, We have placed over their hearts coverings, lest they understand it...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). Akinnah (coverings): plural of kinn, meaning covers. God placed coverings over their hearts, so faith does not enter them and disbelief does not leave them. This is not an oppression by Him toward His servants, exalted is God above that, but rather a response to what they asked for and a fulfilment of what they loved. When they loved disbelief and their chests were expanded by it, He increased them in it, because the Lord gives His servant what he desires. As He said about them in another verse: ﴿In their hearts is a disease, so God increased their disease, and for them is a painful punishment because they used to lie﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:10). And the Exalted said in this meaning: ﴿God has set a seal upon their hearts and upon their hearing, and over their eyes is a veil...﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 2:7).

The meaning of ﴿lest they understand it﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): that is, lest they comprehend it, comprehend the signs of God, because they had already been reminded of them and turned away from them, so God deprived them of understanding and comprehension of it. His saying, the Exalted: ﴿and in their ears is deafness﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): that is, deafness, so they do not hear.

﴿And if you call them to guidance, they will never be guided, ever﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): This is a natural matter, after God has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and blocked off the channels of knowledge and guidance from them, because guidance arises from hearing a word of truth, so that your heart receives it with acceptance, and your limbs are moved to commitment by it. You hear with the ear, accept with the heart, and are moved by the limbs in obedience and commitment to what you have been commanded.

As long as there is deafness and heaviness in the ear, you will not hear, and if you do hear something the heart rejects, the limbs do not act except by what the heart has been charged with of beliefs.

So, it is among the mercies of God toward the disbelievers that He did not hasten to punish them with a torment that would uproot them. Rather, He granted them respite and left them alone, because they have an appointed time from which they cannot flee, nor escape, and they will have no refuge that could protect them from it. There is no doubt that in His granting them respite in this world there is a far-reaching wisdom of God, and perhaps God will bring forth from the loins of these people one who will believe in Him, and who will carry the banner of the religion and defend it. This has happened often in the history of Islam: from the loins of Abu Jahl came ʿIkrimah, and God granted respite to Khalid ibn al-Walid, who became the greatest commander in Islam.

Tilka: a demonstrative particle for the feminine, referring to "the towns" (al-qura), and the kaf is for address. The address here is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and his community is included within his address, because the address to the Messenger is an address to his community. However, a demonstrative is only used for something known, existing and perceptible, as in His saying ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha, 17). So where are these towns, and did they have existence in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ)?

Yes, these towns had traces and ruins that testify to them, which the Prophet (ﷺ) saw, and which people see on their journeys to al-Sham and elsewhere, such as the towns of Thamud, the people of Salih, and the towns of the people of Lut. And Allah the Exalted said about them:

﴿And indeed you pass by them in the morning, and by night. Will you not then reason?﴾ (Surah As-Saffat, 137-138).

So, "tilka" is a reference to something existing and perceptible, whose remnants indicate what befell these towns of the punishment of Allah, and what came upon them of His might, which is not turned back from the wrongdoing people.

The word (al-qura) is the plural of qarya (town), and it is applied to a place in which the necessities of life and its essentials are available, indeed in which there is more than the essentials and the ordinary means of life; because the word qarya is applied only to a place whose means of life are abundant enough to suffice whoever arrives there as a guest, so that he finds provision in it. If it is a large town to which abundant provision comes from every place, it is as if it were a mother, and we call it (Umm al-Qura, the Mother of Towns).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi (surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66)) on surah 18, verse 60:

Allah's words: ﴿And when Musa said to his young man...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:60): That is, mention, O Muhammad, the time when Musa said to his young man. The young man (fata) of Musa was his servant, Yusha' ibn Nun. He was of the lineage of Yusuf, peace be upon him, and he would follow him and serve him so that he could learn from him.

﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:60): But what is the account of Musa with his young man? And what is its relevance to the discussion here?

The relevance of the story of Musa here is that the disbelievers of Makkah sent to the Jews of Madinah asking them about the news of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him, because they were People of the Book and more knowledgeable about the heavenly revelations. So they wanted their opinion about Muhammad: was he truthful or not? The Jews said to the delegation from Makkah: "Ask him three things, and if he answers you, then he is a prophet: ask him about the youths who went off in ancient times, and about the wandering man who traveled the lands, and about the Spirit." So they asked the Messenger of Allah these questions, and he said to them: "Tomorrow I will answer you."

So the answer to these questions was not with him, and this counts in his favour, not against him. For if Muhammad, peace and blessings be upon him, were to speak without knowledge, he would have answered them. But he remained silent until the answer came from Allah, the Exalted, and this is from his good manners, peace and blessings be upon him, with his Lord, who disciplined him and perfected his discipline.

Fifteen days passed without any revelation coming to the Messenger of Allah concerning that, until the matter weighed heavily upon him, and the disbelievers and the hypocrites rejoiced, because they found a handle against the Messenger of Allah, so they seized this opportunity to denounce the Messenger of Allah. Yet Allah's discipline of His Messenger is above everything, to make clear to them that the Messenger of Allah will not speak on this matter except by revelation from Allah, for "he does not speak from desire, nor does his speech come from his own opinion."

Had these people possessed minds, they would have understood that the delay in this matter is proof of the truthfulness of the Prophet, peace and blessings be upon him. Therefore the story of Musa came here to refute the mockery of these people, and to show them that the Prophet does not know everything. Is it required of him that he answer you about everything? Does it diminish his station that he does not know a certain matter?

These verses came to say to the Jews and to whoever resembled them among the disbelievers of Makkah: You are partisan toward Musa, the Torah, and Judaism, and behold, Musa is learning, not from Allah directly but from a servant like himself, walking behind him as a follower in pursuit of knowledge. The verses came to say to them: O you who taught the disbelievers of Makkah these questions and displayed gloating over Muhammad when revelation was delayed to him, know that the delay of revelation is so that you may know that Muhammad does not say anything from his own self. It was therefore incumbent upon you that this matter should direct you to the truthfulness and trustworthiness of Muhammad, and he is not stingy with the unseen.

It is said that the cause of the story of Musa, peace be upon him, is that he asked Allah, and he had a familiarity with his Lord: ﴿My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look at You...﴾ (Surah al-A'raf 7:143). What encouraged him in this request was that Allah spoke to him: ﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha 20:17). So Musa prolonged his speech with his Lord. And who is it that Allah speaks to and does not prolong the enjoyment of conversing with the Speech of Allah? Therefore Musa said: ﴿It is my staff; I lean upon it and beat down leaves for my sheep, and I have in it other uses.﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha 20:18). Thus Musa prolonged the time of intimacy with Allah and conversation with Him, glory be to Him. Therefore he asked Him: "O Lord, is there on earth anyone more knowledgeable than I?" His Lord, blessed and exalted, answered him: "Yes, on earth there is one who is more knowledgeable than you. Go to the meeting place of the two seas, and there you will find a servant of My servants who is more knowledgeable than you." So Musa took his young man and went to the meeting place of the two seas.

It has been related in a hadith of the Messenger of Allah, peace and blessings be upon him, that Musa, peace be upon him, once delivered a sermon and was asked: "Who is the most knowledgeable?" He said: "I am," meaning among mankind. So Allah informed him: "No, rather on earth there is one who is more knowledgeable than you among mankind," so that Musa, peace be upon him, would not be deceived by what Allah had given him of knowledge. Then He says, exalted is He: ﴿I will not cease until I reach the meeting place of the two seas...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:60): "Lā abraḥ" (I will not cease): that is, I will not leave off. Some think that "lā abraḥ" means: I will not leave my place where I am, but it means: I will not leave off what I am engaged in. So if one is sitting, he does not leave off sitting, and if one is walking, he does not leave off walking. Musa, peace be upon him, said this statement while he was seeking the meeting of the two seas and proceeding toward it, so the meaning is: I will not cease traveling to this place until I reach the meeting place of the two seas.

The root (b-r-ḥ) occurs in the words of Allah in the story of Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿So I will not leave this land until my father permits me...﴾ (Surah Yusuf 12:80). Their eldest said it after Yusuf had taken his brother Benjamin and prevented him from going with them. Here the eldest brother was ashamed to face his father, who had taken from them a covenant and a pledge that they would bring him back and return him to him.

And "majma' al-bahrayn" (the meeting place of the two seas) means: the place where they meet, where they become one sea, just as the Tigris and the Euphrates meet at Shatt al-Arab for example. As for His words: ﴿Or I will journey on for a long period (ḥuqub)...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:60): "Ḥuqub" is the plural of ḥiqbah, which is a long period of time. They estimated it at about seventy or eighty years. If the least plural is three, then that means Musa, peace be upon him, would travel two hundred and ten years, on the basis that a ḥiqbah is seventy years.

The meaning is: I will not cease traveling to this place even if I travel two hundred and ten years, because Musa, peace be upon him, was eager to see this man who was more knowledgeable than him. How could he not be, when he is the Prophet and Messenger to whom Allah revealed? Therefore his Lord informed him that the knowledge of this man is knowledge from Our presence, knowledge from Allah, not from mankind.

(Musa and his servant) "reached the meeting-place of the two seas" (that is, the meeting-place of the two seas), "and they forgot their fish" (that is, the forgetting came upon both of them together), although the carrying of the fish had been entrusted to Musa's servant, and he was the one who forgot it. It was incumbent upon Musa to remind him of it, for the leader of a people must be alert to every detail of the caravan. It was the custom that he be the last to leave the place, so that he could check on everyone and see whether someone had forgotten something. Accordingly, it was incumbent upon Musa to follow up an hour after they rose to continue the journey and to remind his servant of the provisions of the journey they had with them.

The hut (al-hut) is a known type of fish; in some countries every fish is called a hut. They had prepared it for eating when they became hungry during the journey, and the servant used to carry it grilled in a basket (maktal). As for the words of Allah, exalted is He, ﴿So it took its way into the sea, as in a tunnel﴾ (Surat al-Kahf 18:61 — note: quoted verse, as cited in the commentary as 60): the grilled fish leapt out of the basket and slipped away toward the sea. The sarab (tunnel) is like a tunnel or an underground passage, or it means a downward slope, just as we say "the water seeped out of the waterskin," for example; that is because the water level in the waterskin is higher, so it seeps out of it. This is among the wonders of the signs: that a grilled fish should leap, regain life, and head toward the sea, because it knows that water is its dwelling and its place.

Meaning: they went beyond the meeting place of the two seas, the place of the appointment. Musa (peace be upon him) said to his servant: "Bring us our morning meal, for we have indeed suffered fatigue from this journey." Al-nasab (نصب) is al-tacb (التعب), i.e., weariness.

So the meaning is that they travelled until they reached the meeting place of the two seas, then rested. When they passed this place, exhaustion and fatigue appeared upon them, and therefore Musa asked for food. Here the young man (al-fata) remembered what had happened with the fish, namely that he had forgotten it.

This is the speech of Musa's young man: "Do you see? Tell me, when we took refuge at the rock at the meeting place of the two seas to rest: ﴿Then indeed I forgot the fish...﴾ [18:63]. We note that here he said "forgot" (nasiytu), while in the previous verse he said ﴿forgot it...﴾ [18:61]."

That is because the first is an account from Allah, and the second is the speech of Musa's young man. The speech of Allah, blessed and exalted is He, shows us that a leader who is followed does not leave his follower to act freely in everything, because the follower may not be concerned with the matter of the journey at all, and his mind may be occupied with other things that make him forget what he is charged with regarding the trip.

Then the young man apologizes for what came from him, the forgetting of the fish, and says: ﴿And none made me forget it except Satan, that I should mention it...﴾ [18:63].

The Satan is the one who played with his thoughts and impulses until he made him forget his duty and made him forget mentioning the fish. And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and it took its way into the sea, marvelously﴾ [18:63]: that is, the fish took its path into the sea in a marvelous manner. In the previous verse He said ﴿a passage﴾ [18:61], and this is the condition of the fish. Here He says "marvelously" because he is recounting what happened and marvelling at it, and how the roasted fish, life stirred in it so that it leapt into the basket and headed toward the water. This is truly one of the wonders, because it came out of the ordinary.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 64:

Ay (that is): Musa (peace be upon him) said: ﴿That is what we were seeking﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:64). Ay: we were seeking. So this is the place where the fish was lost, and it is the intended place. It is as if the fish knew the appointed meeting better than Musa did. Thus the landmark of the place became known: it is Majma' al-Bahrayn (the Meeting Place of the Two Seas), where the two seas meet and become one sea.

This scene exists only in the arena of the Children of Israel in Sinai. There are the Gulf of Aqaba and the Gulf of Suez, which meet in one sea at Ras Muhammad. Then the Exalted says: ﴿So they went back, retracing their footsteps, [carefully]﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:64). Ay: they returned along their own footprints, as trackers do, and the meaning of ﴿qasasan﴾ (carefully/retracing their steps) is:

Ay: with precision, until they reached the place where the fish had slipped away, which is the appointed place that God the Exalted set for Musa (peace be upon him), where he would find there the righteous servant.

Earlier we spoke about servitude ('ubudiyyah). If it is to God, Exalted is He, then it is honour and nobility; if it is to other than God, then it is humiliation and degradation. We said that the Prophet (ﷺ) only attained the favour of the Night Journey and the Ascension (al-Isra' wal-Mi'raj) because he was a servant of God, as He, glorified is He, said: ﴿Glory be to the One who took His servant by night...﴾ (Surah al-Isra'). Just as in servitude to God the servant receives the goodness of his Master, so in servitude to human beings the master receives the goodness of his servant.

Then the Truth, glorified is He, described this righteous servant, saying: ﴿We had given him mercy from Us...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 65). The scholars have spoken about the meaning of mercy (rahmah) here. They said: mercy in the Qur'an has come with the meaning of prophethood, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they say, "Why was this Qur'an not sent down upon a man of importance from the two cities?"﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf, 31).

So God's response to them was: ﴿Is it they who would apportion the mercy of your Lord?...﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf, 32), meaning: prophethood. General mercy comes through the hand of Gabriel, peace be upon him, and through the hand of the messengers. But this mercy is from Us directly, without the intermediary of the angel. Therefore He, Exalted, said: ﴿We had given him...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 65), (We being the speaker), and He said: ﴿from Us...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 65). So the giving and the "from-ness" are from God directly.

Then He says after it: ﴿and taught him knowledge from Our presence﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 65), meaning: from Us, not through the messengers. Therefore they call it 'ilm ladunni (knowledge from the divine presence), as if there is no impediment for God, Exalted, to choose a servant from among His servants and bestow upon him a special knowledge beyond prophethood.

Therefore, we must distinguish between knowledge and outpourings that come through the Messenger and his guidance, and knowledge and outpourings that come from God, Exalted, directly to whomever He chooses from among His servants. For the Messenger brings outward rulings concerning obligations: do this and do not do that. But there are other rulings, not outward, which have inner causes beyond the outward causes, and these are what God singled out this righteous servant (al-Khidr) with, as the Prophet (ﷺ) named him.

The proof of this is that the Prophet brings rulings forbidding killing and forbidding the destruction of another's property. Al-Khidr came and damaged the ship and killed the boy, and Musa, peace be upon him, objected to these actions because he had no knowledge of their cause. Had Musa, peace be upon him, known the cause of puncturing the ship, he would himself have hastened to puncture it.

Therefore, the knowledge of Musa is other than the knowledge of al-Khidr; for this reason he said to him: ﴿Indeed, you will not be able to have patience with me﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 67), and ﴿And how can you have patience about that which you have not encompassed in knowledge?﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 68). This is knowledge you do not have. My knowledge is from the purse of walaya (sainthood), and your knowledge is from the purse of the messengers. In reality the two do not contradict each other, though the knowledge of walaya has inner causes, and the knowledge of risalah has outward causes.

Al-Sha'rawi's commentary on Surah 18, verse 66:

It is as if Musa (peace be upon him) is teaching us the etiquette of receiving knowledge and the etiquette of the student with his teacher. Although Allah Most High had commanded him to follow al-Khidr, he did not say to him, for example, "Allah has commanded me to follow you." Rather, he was gentle with him and asked his permission in this manner: ﴿May I follow you...﴾ [18:66]

Al-rushd (right guidance, maturity of judgment) is the good handling of matters and the soundness of course in the cause of what you are concerned with. We have said before that rushd occurs at the age of maturity, but this does not mean that everyone who reaches maturity is rightly guided. A person may be mature and yet not rightly guided; he may be a fool (safih). Therefore, when the Truth, glorified is He, spoke about orphans, He said: ﴿And test the orphans...﴾ [4:6]; that is, test them. The testing of the orphan takes place during his orphanhood, while he is still under your guardianship. You must assign him a task that will improve his condition, and give him a portion of his wealth to manage under your eye and your care, so that you may see how he will conduct himself.

You must be keen to train him to face life, and not keep him isolated from it until he reaches rushd, and then hand him his wealth, whereupon he cannot manage it for lack of experience. If he fails, the trial was conducted with his wealth and the loss falls upon him.

So, the testing of the orphan takes place while he is still under your guardianship and within your hearing and sight, in safeguarding his right.

﴿And when they reach marriageable age...﴾ [4:6]; that is, the age of puberty. He did not say after it, "then hand over their wealth to them," because after puberty there is another condition: ﴿then if you perceive in them rushd...﴾ [4:6]. So the guardian must observe this order:

You must care for the orphan while he is under your guardianship, and send him into the struggle of life and its experiences, until he is able to face life and does not flounder with his wealth for lack of experience and expertise. If you know his rushd after puberty, hand over his wealth to him so that he may manage it; but if you do not perceive in him rushd and good management, do not leave him the wealth to squander through his poor conduct. On this meaning, the Most High says: ﴿And do not give the foolish your wealth...﴾ [4:5]. He did not say "their wealth," because the fool has no wealth during his foolishness; rather, it is your wealth, so that you may manage it well and keep it for its owner until you are certain of his rushd.

So, the rushd that Musa sought from the righteous servant is soundness of conduct and wisdom in dealing with things. But does this mean that Musa (peace be upon him) was not rightly guided? No; rather, he was rightly guided in his own path as a Messenger, rightly guided in conveying the outward rulings.

As for the rushd he sought, it is the rushd in the path of the righteous servant, and this indicates that he sought something that was not known to him. This does not detract from the station of prophethood, because the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, said: ﴿And you have not been given of knowledge except a little﴾ [17:85].

And He said to the Prophet (ﷺ): ﴿And say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge"﴾ [20:114].

Therefore the poet says:

The more knowledge I acquire, the more I become certain of my ignorance.

For the meaning of his having increased in knowledge today is that he was deficient yesterday, and likewise he is deficient today so that he may learn tomorrow.

When a person is broad in outlook and loves knowledge, you will see that whenever he learns one matter he longs for another; he is in constant craving for knowledge and is never satisfied with it, as the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Two insatiable appetites: the seeker of knowledge and the seeker of wealth."

And the poet who was alert to himself, when his soul invited him to conceit, pride, and vanity over the little knowledge he had, yet was watchful of its deception, said:

The soul said, "You have come to know much."
I said, "This much is but a small sip."

Then he gave a illustrative example:

The jug fills with a handful from the ocean,
and it thinks itself the great ocean.

Here the righteous servant begins to set out the conditions of this companionship, and he makes clear to Musa, peace be upon him, the nature of his knowledge and his way. "Your way is not my way, and my knowledge comes from a bag other than your bag, and you will see from me actions you will not be able to bear patiently, because you have no knowledge of their inner realities." It is as though he is seeking to excuse himself in advance for not being patient with him.

Then do not grieve, for I said: you will not be able to have patience with me; because the actions you will object to are things you have no knowledge of. And how can you be patient with something you have no knowledge of?

We note in this dialogue between Musa and al-Khidr, peace be upon them, the etiquette of dialogue and the difference of opinion between two methods: the method of outward rulings (al-ahkam al-zahiriyyah), and the method of what lies behind outward rulings, and that each of them accepts the opinion of the other, respects it, and does not object to it or deny it. This is unlike what we see among adherents of different schools (madhahib), where some deny others and even declare one another to be unbelievers. When they see, for example, a servant of God whom God has chosen with some of His overflowing favours, and who has a path and followers, we see someone who denies it, and the matter may reach insults, disparagement, and even takfir.

In al-Khidr's words ﴿And how can you be patient with that which you do not encompass in knowledge?﴾ (Surat al-Kahf 18:68) there appears a manifestation of the teacher's etiquette toward the student, in that he respected his opinion and sought excuse for him if he objected. Each of them has his own way, and one way may not be used as proof against another. So what did the student say after he listened to these conditions?

Meaning: "I accept your conditions, O teacher, so be at ease; I will not argue with you or oppose you in anything." He placed the will (of God) first and said:

﴿If God wills, you will find me patient﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:69): to win his heart and soften it toward him.

﴿patient﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:68): Thus he made himself one who is commanded, the teacher being the one who commands, and the student the one who is commanded.

This is an affirmation from Khidr to Musa, and an explanation of the manner that must be followed in accompanying him: "If you follow me, then do not ask me about anything until I myself mention it to you." It is as though he is teaching him the etiquette of acquiring knowledge, patience with it, and not being hasty to learn the meaning of each matter separately.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 71:

(So they set off) They went together until they boarded a ship, which was prepared for carrying passengers. Then al-Khidr hastened to damage it and destroy it. At that point Musa could not bear this matter; it weighed heavily on his mind, and he could not be patient with it, so he said: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people? You have certainly done a dreadful thing.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:71). That is: a strange or terrible matter. Musa forgot what he had taken upon himself, namely to obey the righteous servant, not to oppose him, and to be patient with what he saw of his actions.

It is as if the Truthful, Blessed and Exalted God wants to teach us that theoretical speech is one thing, and practical action is another. You may hear from someone a fine statement that pleases you, but when the time for action and implementation comes, you find nothing, because words are sometimes spoken at the outset in the language of generosity, like someone who says to you: "I am at your command, and my neck is yours." But when reality compels you to rely on him, you are like one trying to grasp water, finding nothing of it.

We note here that Musa, peace be upon him, did not content himself with the question: ﴿Have you made a hole in it to drown its people?﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:71). Rather, he went further to accuse him of having committed a reprehensible, terrible matter. This is because Musa's theoretical speech is one thing, and his seeing the ship's damage and destruction without justification is another. For Musa had in mind the legal ruling concerning the destruction of another's property, let alone drowning the passengers of the ship, so he saw the matter as grave and the harm as great. This is because Musa takes from one purse, and al-Khidr takes from another purse.

This is another lesson from al-Khidr to Musa, peace be upon them both. He says: "My words to you were true. I warned you that you would not be patient with what you would see of my actions, and here you are, objecting to me, although we had agreed and taken a pledge that you would not ask me about anything until I myself told you about it."

Musa (peace be upon him) apologizes for what came from him toward his teacher, and asks him to forgive him and not to hold him to account: ﴿And do not burden me, for my matter, with difficulty﴾ [18:73]. That is: do not load me, in the matter of following you, with hardship and difficulty. Then al-Khidr forgave him and they resumed the journey.

Your text is a tafsir commentary, so I'll translate it below.

You notice that the first transgression by al-Khidr was against property that he damaged, whereas here the matter escalates to killing a pure soul without any right. For what offence is this boy killed, one who has not yet reached maturity of judgment? Therefore, in the first instance he said: ﴿Indeed, you have done something terrible (imran)﴾ [18:73], meaning: something strange (ajiban). Here, however, he said: ﴿Indeed, you have done something hideous (nukran)﴾ [18:74], meaning: something reprehensible (munkaran), because the crime is grave.

The "pure soul" (al-nafs al-zakiyya) is the one that is clean and unsullied, not stained by sins or by transgressing the divine obligations. Likewise, al-Khidr's response comes differing from his first response. In the first time he said: ﴿Did I not say that you would not be able to have patience with me?﴾ [18:72], meaning: you were speaking a general statement.

[Translation]

"And he confirmed it and repeated it to him in speech, i.e.: 'Did I not tell you?' Then, after the second time in which Moses interrupts his teacher al-Khidr, he takes a new covenant upon himself."

Thus Musa (peace be upon him) cut off the way for himself, and gave himself one last chance after which the parting would be completed.

So this is the third time, and Musa has no excuse after it. The meaning of ﴿And you have indeed reached from me an excuse﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:76) is: you have done with me everything that can be done, and I have no excuse after this.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 77:

Istat'amahu (asked him for food): that is, asked for food. Asking for food is the most sincere kind of request, for no one asks for food except one who is hungry and in need. Had he asked for money, we would say he was saving it up; but food is not something anyone can object to. Refusing food to one who asks for it is a sign of stinginess and baseness rooted in one's nature. This is what happened with the people of this town, past which they passed and asked for food, and they refused them.

Whoever reflects on the verse finds that the Qur'anic style portrays the extent of these people's stinginess, baseness and evil nature. It does not say, for instance, "fa-abaw an yut'imuhuma" (they refused to feed them). Rather it says: ﴿But they refused to entertain them﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). There is a difference between feeding (it'am) and hospitality (diyafah). "They refused to feed them" means they withheld food from them; but "they refused to entertain them" means everything that could be offered to a guest, even mere lodging and welcome. This is the utmost that can be imagined of these people's baseness. You will also notice the repetition of the word "ahl" (people). When it says ﴿they came to the people of a town﴾ (Surah al-Kahf), the context would call for a pronoun, so one would say "istat'amuhum" (they asked them for food). But it says ﴿they asked the people of it for food﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). Why? Because when they entered the town, did they meet all its people, or did they meet only some of them, those who confronted them as they entered?

Naturally, they met some of them. But the asking for food was directed at all the people of the town, as if they passed by every house in the town and asked its people, one after another, to no avail, as though they were all united in stinginess and baseness of character.

Then the Exalted and Glorified says: ﴿And they found in it a wall about to collapse, so he set it upright﴾ (Surah al-Kahf).

That is, they did not stay long among these base people before they found a wall that wanted to collapse. We know that "wanting" (iradah) belongs only to one who thinks and understands; if it is attributed to one who does not, it carries the meaning of "nearness" (qurb). That is, a wall that was about to fall down, because of signs we see in it, such as cracks and fissures.

This understanding suits those of superficial thinking and narrow horizons. As for those of broad horizons, who give the intellect its role in thought and contemplation and examine matters closely, they have no objection to the wall having a will, on the basis that everything in the cosmos has a life suited to it, and God the Exalted may address it and there may be speech between them.

Did not the Exalted say: ﴿So the sky and the earth did not weep over them﴾ (Surah al-Dukhan)? If the sky weeps, it has gone beyond mere speech, and it has feelings and sentiments, and it has affections that may rise above human affections. So His saying ﴿so the sky and the earth did not weep over them﴾ (Surah al-Dukhan) is evidence that they weep over the loss of the righteous.

Imam Ali (may Allah be pleased with him) was asked about this matter and said: "Yes. When a believer dies, two places weep over him: a place on the earth and a place in the sky. As for his place on the earth, it is the place where he prayed; as for his place in the sky, it is the ascent of his deeds."

This is evidence of the harmony of the believing servant with the cosmos around him. The cosmos prostrates to God, glorifies God, obeys God, loves the obedient, and repels and hates and curses the disobedient. Therefore the Arabs say "nabaa bihi al-makan" (the place repelled him), meaning he disliked it, because he was not in harmony with it. The place is obedient while he is disobedient; the place glorifies while he is heedless. On this understanding, the saying of the Exalted ﴿wanting to collapse﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) is to be taken literally.

So these creatures have perception and have weeping, and they grieve over the loss of loved ones. In a hadith, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, I know a stone in Makkah that used to greet me before I was commissioned."

It is narrated in the biography (sirah) that the trunk of a palm tree yearned for the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), and that pebbles glorified in his hand (ﷺ). We have already explained this matter before, saying: one should not say "the pebbles glorified in the hand of the Messenger of Allah," because the pebbles also glorify in the hand of Abu Jahl; rather, we say: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) heard the glorification of the pebbles in his hands.

It is no wonder that the Qur'an gives us examples of the speech of these things. We have seen scholars in the modern age researching a language for fish, a language for birds, and a language for bats, from which they derived the idea of radar. Indeed, they have reached the conclusion that animals sense the occurrence of earthquakes, especially donkeys, and that they flee the place just before the earthquake strikes directly. So they have means of perception, they have a language by which they communicate, and they have a logic by which they express themselves.

Then the Exalted says about the deed of Khidr with the wall that was about to collapse: ﴿So he set it upright﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). That is, he repaired it and restored it.

﴿He said: "If you had wished, you could have taken a wage for it."﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) This is the saying of Musa (peace be upon him) when he saw the baseness and meanness of the people. We asked them for food and they did not feed us; they did not even offer us mere shelter. So how should we do this work for them without a wage?

This statement came from Musa (peace be upon him) because he did not know the wisdom behind this action.

(Al-)Qala (he said) — i.e., the righteous servant (al-'abd al-salih) — "This" — i.e., what occurred from you, namely your saying: ﴿If you had willed, you could have taken a wage for it.﴾

(Surah al-Kahf): Musa, peace be upon him, had earlier stipulated upon himself that if he objected to his teacher this time, separation would occur between them. It is as though the righteous servant had brought nothing of his own; Musa had said: ﴿If I ask you about anything after this, do not keep me in your company.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf)

His saying: ﴿This is a parting between me and you.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) — this is considered a constitution (dustur) from the Truth, glorified and exalted be He, and an indication that these two paths do not meet: each of them keeps its own way. The one who has undergone spiritual discipline (al-murtad) has a way, and the one who has not undergone it has his way. Neither should object to the other; rather, each must observe his etiquette within the limits of what God has taught him. Then the Exalted says on the tongue of al-Khidr: ﴿I will inform you of the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) — i.e., I will not leave you with these questions in your soul, so that nothing about me remains in your heart. I will inform you of the reality of these actions which you objected to, so that you may know that God did not deceive you, but sent you to one who would teach you something you did not know.

Then the righteous servant began to reveal to Musa the wisdom behind these actions, one after another, just as when your companion reproaches you about some matter while you are keen on his affection, and you say to him: "Give me time to explain to you what happened; I did such-and-such for such-and-such a reason," so as to ease his heart and remove what has become confused for him in this matter.

They have said: this is from the etiquette of companionship. It is not permissible, after companionship, that we part in disagreement; we should part in harmony and contentment, because parting in disagreement increases the rift and invites estrangement. Therefore: before we part, the matter is such-and-such, so that affairs become clear and souls become pure.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 79:

Allah's words: (لمساكين) "to the poor (masakin)." The lam here indicates ownership (al-milkiyyah), meaning that the boat belonged to them. This verse settles the scholarly disagreement over the definitions of the faqir (the poor person) and the miskin (the needy person), and over which of the two is in greater need than the other. Accordingly, the miskin is one who owns something that does not suffice him, like these people who owned a boat that worked at sea, and the Qur'an called them masakin. As for the faqir, he is one who owns nothing.

The meaning of ﴿they work on the sea﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:79): that is, the field of their work is the sea, where they work by carrying passengers or goods, or fishing, or other such things.

His words: ﴿so I wished to damage it﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:79).

The speaker here is al-Khidr, peace be upon him. He attributed the wish to damage the boat to himself and did not attribute it to Allah, exalting Allah above what is unbecoming. But in matters of good he attributed the matter to Allah, saying: ﴿So your Lord intended that they reach their maturity and extract their treasure﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:82). Therefore, at the end of the story, he returns everything he did to Allah, saying: ﴿And I did it not of my own accord﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:82).

Then Allah, exalted is He, says: ﴿And there was behind them a king who seized every boat by force﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:79).

The word "every" (kull) draws a comprehensive general rule that leaves nothing out. So the intended meaning is that he seizes every boat, whether it is defective or not. In reality, however, he seizes only the boat that is fit for use, and he has no need for a defective boat that is unfit. It is as if the context of the verse implies an implied qualification: that is, he seizes every fit boat by force from its owner.

Al-ghasb (usurpation): what is taken without right, by force, compulsion, and confiscation. It has several forms, such as theft (al-sariqah), which is taking property from its safe place secretly, like breaking into a cabinet or a strongbox. Another is ghasb (usurpation) in the narrower sense, which is taking another's property by force, in plain sight. In this case a struggle and a confrontation occur between the usurper and the one whose property is taken. Another is khatf (snatching), which is taking another's property openly but by some trick: one snatches the thing and flees with it so that you cannot catch up with him. Snatching therefore happens openly but without resistance. Another is ikhtilas (embezzlement), which is taking another's property while you are entrusted with it. Embezzlement happens secretly and does not lack a trick that conceals it.

Since the matter here is usurpation, the owner of the thing must resist, even if only to a limited degree, defending his right, and he may plead with the usurper to leave his property to him. The matter therefore involves argument and counter-argument.

Thus: damaging the boat, on its outward appearance, is an assault on a valued property, and this is forbidden by the Shari'ah. But if this assault will be the cause of saving the whole boat from the usurper, then there is no harm in it, and a defective boat is better than no boat. Had Musa, peace be upon him, known this wisdom, he would have hastened to damage it himself.

Since the matter is so, we must turn the boat into one that is unfit and make it defective by damaging it, or by removing a plank from it, so as to divert the attention of the usurping king from seizing it.

The word ﴿behind them﴾ (wara'ahum) here means "in front of them," because this wrongdoer was lying in wait for the boats that passed by him; whenever he found one fit, he seized it. So in reality he was in front of them, in the same way as Allah's words: ﴿Behind him is Hell, and he is given to drink of festering water﴾ (Surah Ibrahim 14:16). Is Hell behind him or in front of him? Wara' is used in the sense of "after," as in Allah's words: ﴿And We gave her good news of Isaac, and after Isaac, Jacob﴾ (Surah Hud 11:71). It also comes in the sense of "other than," as in Allah's words describing the believers: ﴿And those who guard their private parts, except from their spouses or what their right hands possess, for indeed they are not blamed. But whoever seeks beyond that, it is those who are the transgressors﴾ (Surah al-Mu'minun 23:5–7).

And in Allah's words: ﴿Prohibited to you are your mothers...﴾ (Surah an-Nisa 4:23) up to ﴿and lawful to you is what is beyond that﴾ (Surah an-Nisa 4:24). Wara' is also sometimes used in the sense of "behind," as in Allah's words: ﴿But they cast it behind their backs﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran 3:187).

Therefore, the word wara' has come in the Qur'an with four meanings: in front of, behind, after, other than. This is one of the features that distinguishes Arabic from other languages, and the Arabic linguistic faculty is able to discern the meaning appropriate to the context. The word "ayn," for example, comes to mean the eye that sees, or the spring of water, or gold and silver, or a spy. It is the context that determines the intended meaning.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 80:

Al-ghulam (the boy): the child who has not yet reached puberty (al-hulm) and the age of legal responsibility (al-taklif). As long as he has not been made responsible, he remains in the age of purity and innocence from sins. Therefore, when Musa objected to his killing, he said: ﴿Have you killed an innocent soul without [its having killed] another?﴾ [18:74]

That is, pure (tahira). There is no doubt that taking the boy at this age is better for him and in his interest, before sins defile him and he enters the sphere of reckoning.

So, his purity is what prompted us to hasten his taking. This concerns the boy; what, then, of his father and mother?

The Exalted says: ﴿And his parents were believers﴾ [18:80]. Children often become a trial (fitnah) for their parents, as the Exalted said: ﴿O you who believe, indeed among your spouses and your children there are enemies to you, so beware of them﴾ [64:14]. The trial through children comes from the parents' eagerness for them and their striving to put them in the best condition. Sometimes resources are insufficient, so the father is compelled to take what is forbidden for the sake of his children. The Exalted God knew that this boy would be a trial for his parents, while they were believers, and God did not want trial for them. He decreed that He take them to Himself in a state of faith.

It is as if God's decree came as good for the boy and good for the parents, a favor bestowed upon both of them, and a profound wisdom hidden behind the apparent event over which Musa, peace be upon him, objected.

Therefore, it is foolish, when a small child or young boy dies among us, for grief over him to become intense, lamenting his lost childhood and the youth he never enjoyed. We do not know what bliss has been prepared for him. We do not know that one who is taken from our children before puberty is not assigned a fixed dwelling in Paradise, because all of it is his: he moves about in it as he wishes and sits wherever he likes. He sits with the prophets and with the Companions, and no one stops him. For this reason they are called "the darting ones of Paradise" (da'ami al-jannah).

Then the Exalted says: ﴿We feared that he would overburden them with transgression and disbelief﴾ [18:80]. Khashina (we feared): we were apprehensive. One of us has a son born to him who becomes a source of joy and support, and yet this son may become a cause of the corruption of his father's religion, leading him to lying, bribery and theft. This son drags his father toward the Fire, and it is better that God remove such a child from the path of the parent so that he does not transgress.

Al-Khidr, peace be upon him, does not fail to attribute the good here too to God. He says: "I love this work and desire it," but in reality it is God, exalted is He, who replaces them: ﴿So We desired that their Lord would replace them with one better than him in purity⁠﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). This good is from God, and I am only a means to achieving it. And His saying: ﴿better than him in purity⁠﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): that is, in cleanliness (tahara).

﴿and nearer in mercy⁠﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): because the two of them wanted a child who would benefit them in this world and be a comfort to their eyes. Since this world is a trial with no permanence, and it was established in His knowledge, exalted is He, that this child would be a trial for his two parents, would bring upon them sins and misdeeds, and would drag them into punishment, the complete mercy lay in taking him, instead of their enjoying him in the transient world and being miserable with him in the everlasting Hereafter.

(لغلامين) That is, they had not yet reached the age of maturity (rushd), and moreover they were orphans. Beneath this leaning wall lay a treasure belonging to these two boys, who were unable to manage their own affairs. You may imagine what would have happened had the wall collapsed and this treasure been exposed, its gold gleaming before the eyes of those people whose character you know, who had denied them food and even mere shelter. The least that can be said of them is that they are base people who cannot be trusted with anything. We are accustomed to express the severity of neglect by saying: "The orphans' loss at the tables of the base."

So there is no doubt that what the righteous servant did, in building and restoring the wall, was a slap in the face for those base people, fitting the denial and bad reception they had shown, and a repayment in kind, measure for measure, for the way they had deprived the boys of this treasure.

The reason for repairing the wall was the wealth beneath it, which had to be preserved until these two boys grew up and became able to safeguard and protect it in a village of base people. It is as though the Almighty sent him to these two boys at this very time, when the wall had begun to crack and showed signs of collapse, so that he would repair it before it fell and the matter of the treasure and its owners was exposed while they were weak and unable to protect it.

Then the righteous servant repaired the wall and restored it to its former state, as one whom God had taught from His own presence.
