It is said that he built it as a time-limited structure suited to the age of the two boys, as though he built it on a hypothetical lifespan that would end when the two boys reached the age of maturity and the ability to protect the treasure, whereupon it would collapse. In reality, this is a precise operation, and no one can calculate it except one who has been given special knowledge by God Most High.

It appears from the context of the verse that they were of the same age, twins, based on the words of God Most High: ﴿So your Lord desired that they reach their maturity⦆ [18:82]. That is: that they become strong and sound. The meaning of ashudd (maturity) is strength, when the body's faculties are complete and balanced, and the faculties of the body are complete when a person becomes able to father offspring like himself. And you notice that God Most High said here ﴿that they reach their maturity⦆ [18:82] and did not say "their rushd," because there is a difference between rushd and ashudd: rushd is sound judgment in affairs, whereas ashudd is strength. The two boys here needed the strength that would protect their treasure from these base people, so ashudd fits here: ﴿their maturity⦆ [18:82].

Then God Most High says: ﴿and they extract their treasure as a mercy from your Lord⦆ [18:82]. That is: they extract it by the strength and vigor they possess. Mercy (rahmah) is a quality that is given to the one who receives mercy in order to protect him from harm, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿And We send down of the Qur'an that which is a healing and a mercy for the believers⦆ [17:82]. So His words "healing" mean that it cures an existing ailment and restores health, and "mercy" means a mercy that prevents the ailment from returning. Likewise, what happened to these two boys was a mercy from God to protect their wealth and safeguard their right. Then the righteous servant did not neglect to attribute the grace to its people, and to deny for himself any conceit in knowledge or superiority over his companion, so he says: ﴿And I did not do it of my own accord⦆ [18:82]. That is: what happened was by the command of God, and what I taught you was from God. So I have no advantage over you, and this is a lesson in the manners of humility and in acknowledging grace to those who deserve it. Then He says: ﴿That is the interpretation of that over which you could not hold patience⦆ [18:82]. Ta'wil means returning a matter to its reality and explaining what was obscure in it. After this, the verses move to another of the three questions that the disbelievers of Makkah asked the Messenger of God at the instigation of the Jews, namely the question about the wandering man who traveled the lands:

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 83:

Dhu al-Qarnayn (the Two-Horned): this is his epithet. It may be because he was physically two-horned, or because he wore a crown with two sides, or because he reached the two horns of the sun, in the east and in the west.

The scholars have investigated: who is Dhu al-Qarnayn? Some of them said: he is Alexander the Great of Macedon, who travelled through the lands. But Alexander the Great was in Macedonia in the west, whereas Dhu al-Qarnayn traversed the east and the west. This led a scholar of research from India, namely Abu al-Kalam Azad, the Indian Minister of Education, to say that he is not Alexander the Great but rather Cyrus the Righteous. This is his journey in the east and the west and between the two barriers. Moreover, Alexander was a polytheist and a student of Aristotle, whereas Dhu al-Qarnayn was a believing man, as we shall know from his story.

In general, it is not in the interest of the story to confine it to a specific person, because identifying the event of the story weakens its impact and colours it with a personal hue that does not extend to others, so that we see someone saying that it is a personal matter that is not repeated.

Therefore: if knowledge came in its own right, we would say: this event or this deed is specific to this person. But Allah the Exalted wants to set forth for us an example that applies to any person: what would be his conduct and behaviour if Allah empowered him and granted him strength and authority?

And if the Qur'an had specified this personality as Alexander or Cyrus or someone else, we would say: it is an individual event that does not extend beyond this person, and the soul would turn away from taking him as a model, and the story would lose its meaning and impact. Had identifying him been of benefit, Allah would have made him known to us.

We have previously explained that when Allah the Exalted set forth an example for those who disbelieved, He said: ﴿The wife of Noah and the wife of Lot﴾ (Surah al-Tahrim), and did not specify them precisely, because the purpose of the example here is to show that the messenger sent by Allah to guide people could not guide his own wife and the person nearest to him, since faith is a personal matter in which no one has control over anyone else. Likewise, when Allah set forth an example for those who believed, He said: ﴿The wife of Pharaoh﴾ (Surah al-Tahrim). Pharaoh, who led people astray and claimed divinity, had a wife who was a believer. It is as if Allah the Exalted is hinting to all people that your opinion regarding religion and beliefs is a personal opinion, not affected by anyone whoever he may be: neither by guidance from a prophet, nor by error from the most misguided of the astray, who claimed divinity.

Thus Islam preserves for the woman her role and capacity and respects her opinion.

Therefore: Allah the Exalted brought this story without specifying its figures so that it would be a model and example that everyone can follow. Otherwise, had it been specified, it would have been tied to that person alone and not to others. As for when the Exalted spoke of Mary, He specified her by name, and even the name of her father, because what would happen to Mary is a matter particular to her, and will never happen again among the daughters of Adam; therefore He specified and identified her, since specification is necessary in such a situation.

As for when the example or story is left without specification, this means that it is suitable to recur at any time or in any place, as we saw in the story of the People of the Cave, and how Allah the Exalted left their names unspecified, their place unspecified, their time unspecified, and their number unspecified, so that they would be a model and exemplar for believing youths at any time, in any place, and with any number.

And His saying: ﴿They ask you concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 83). We note that the matter of questioning the Messenger of Allah ﷺ occupies a large space in the Qur'an. The question was addressed to the Prophet by the people sixteen times, one of them in the past tense in the words of the Exalted: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 186).

And fifteen times in the present tense, as in: ﴿They ask you concerning the new moons﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 189).

And His saying: ﴿They ask you what they should spend. Say: Whatever good you spend is for parents﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 215).

﴿They ask you concerning the sacred month, about fighting therein﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 217).

﴿They ask you concerning wine and gambling﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 219).

﴿And they ask you what they should spend. Say: The surplus﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 219).

﴿And they ask you concerning orphans. Say: Reforming them is best﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 220).

﴿And they ask you concerning menstruation﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 222).

﴿They ask you what has been made lawful for them﴾ (Surah al-Ma'idah, 4).

﴿They ask you about the Hour﴾ (Surah al-A'raf, 187).

﴿They ask you about the spoils﴾ (Surah al-Anfal, 1).

﴿And they ask you about the soul﴾ (Surah al-Isra', 85).

﴿And they ask you concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 83).

﴿And they ask you concerning the mountains. Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha, 105).

Fifteen questions in the present tense, yet the answers to them differ, and all of them come from Allah the Wise. The difference in the answer in each question must have a point to it. Among these questions are those posed by opponents, and among them are those posed by believers. The question from the believers to the Messenger of Allah, though he had forbidden them to ask him until they calmed down, reflects their insistence on knowing their conduct, even in the time of ignorance, since they wanted to know Islam's view of it. It is as if they had forgotten the customs of the Age of Ignorance and desired that all their affairs be legislated in accordance with Islam.

On reflecting on the answers to these questions, you find that in one of them the answer comes directly without (Say), and that is in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 186). And one came joined with the particle fa (then Say), which is His saying: ﴿They ask you concerning the mountains, so say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha, 105). The rest of the questions are answered with the verb (Say). So what is the wisdom in the verb being joined with fa in this verse and not in others?

They said: when the Exalted says in the answer (Say), this is an answer to a question that the Messenger actually received, that is, it has actually happened from them. As for the fa, it came in the answer to a question he had not been asked, but would be asked in the future.

So His saying: ﴿They ask you concerning the mountains﴾ (Surah Ta-Ha, 105) is a question that has not yet happened, so the meaning is: if they ask you, then say, as a precaution for an answer to a question that will occur. If you say: what is the wisdom in the answer coming in His saying: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 186), without (Say) or (then say), even though (if/when) requires fa in its answer?

We say: because the question here is about Allah the Exalted, and He wills to answer them about it without any intermediary from anyone; therefore the answer comes directly without an intermediary: ﴿And when My servants ask you concerning Me, indeed I am near, I answer the invocation of the supplicant﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 186).

His saying: ﴿They ask you concerning Dhu al-Qarnayn﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 83), that is: concerning his history, his story, and the mission he carried out. ﴿Say: I will recite to you from him a remembrance﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 83). And what honour is greater than this honour? Allah, blessed and exalted, takes upon Himself the recording of this man's history, and records it in His noble Qur'an, which is recited and worshipped by, up to the Day of Resurrection, and by which He challenges, so that his remembrance remains as long as the Qur'an remains, eternal by its eternity; his impact in what he did remains an example and model for whoever does the like. If it indicates anything, it indicates only that righteous deeds are recorded with Allah before they are recorded among creation.

So what remembrance is more lasting than Allah's remembrance of the report of Dhu al-Qarnayn and his history?

And ﴿minhu﴾ (from him) means: some of his remembrance and history, not all of his history.

The word ﴿dhikr﴾ (remembrance) occurs in the Qur'an with multiple meanings, all of which converge on honour and elevation, and on remembrance and lesson-taking. When used absolutely, it primarily refers to the Qur'an, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, We sent down the Reminder, and indeed, We will be its guardian﴾ (Surah al-Hijr, 9). After that it is used for any book Allah sent down among the earlier scriptures, as in His saying: ﴿And We did not send before you except men to whom We revealed. So ask the people of the Reminder if you do not know﴾ (Surah al-Nahl, 43). The word dhikr is also applied to what follows from it of fame, honour, elevation, and the immortalising of a name, as in His saying: ﴿We have certainly sent down to you a Book in which is your remembrance﴾ (Surah al-Anbiya', 10).

And His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a remembrance for you and your people﴾ (Surah al-Zukhruf, 44): that is, a good reputation, honour, and elevation, because the Qur'an mentions this name, and when a name is mentioned in the Qur'an its fame spreads and resounds across the horizons.

In the story of Zayd ibn Harithah, we mentioned that he was a slave after he had been kidnapped from his people and sold in Mecca to Khadijah (may Allah be pleased with her), then she gave him to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ; therefore they called him Zayd ibn Muhammad. When his family learnt of his presence in Mecca, his father and his uncle came and spoke to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ about Zayd, and he said: give him the choice.

When they gave Zayd the choice, he said: I would never choose anyone over the Messenger of Allah. Therefore the Prophet ﷺ honoured him and named him Zayd ibn Muhammad. Then, when Allah the Exalted willed to abolish adoption, there came His saying: ﴿Muhammad is not the father of any of your men, but he is the Messenger of Allah and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 40).

And He said: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; it is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 5). So do not say: Zayd ibn Muhammad, but say: Zayd ibn Harithah. Here Zayd grieved over this change, and saw that he had lost a great honour by his attribution to Muhammad. But Allah the Exalted consoles Zayd's heart, and makes his name a标 known banner recited in a Qur'an that is recited and worshipped up to the Day of Resurrection. Zayd was thus the only companion whose name is mentioned by name in the Book of Allah, in His saying: ﴿So when Zayd had no more need for her, We married her to you﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 37). What honour is higher and greater than this honour? And we note in this verse: ﴿Call them by [the names of] their fathers; it is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 5).

﴿Say: I will recite to you from him a remembrance﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 83): that Allah the Exalted did not accuse His Messenger ﷺ of injustice, so He said: ﴿It is more just in the sight of Allah﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 5). Thus what the Messenger did was also justice and fairness, and what Allah commanded is the most just and the most equitable.

Therefore, the mention of Dhu al-Qarnayn in the Book of Allah is a great honour, and an indication that the doer of good has his station and rank with Allah, and is rewarded with having his remembrance immortalised and his fame remaining among people in this world.

Empowerment: that is, We gave him capabilities by which he could carry out all the affairs he wished, because he was trusted to manage affairs according to the method of God, as God the Exalted said in another verse about Yusuf, peace be upon him: ﴿And thus did We establish Yusuf in the land, to take residence therein wherever he willed...﴾ (Surah Yusuf, 56). So empowerment means giving him capabilities for every purpose he wants, so that he manages affairs through them. But why did We empower him? We empowered him because he is trusted to manage affairs according to the method of God, and trusted with the capabilities God gave him. And His saying: ﴿And We gave him of every thing a means﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 84): that is, We gave him means by which he reaches what he wants, for there is nothing he wants except that God makes for him a means leading to it. So what did he do?

Follow the cause (sabab); that is, he did not set out toward any goal except by the means that God had made available to him. For God had established Dhu al-Qarnayn firmly in the earth and had given him a means (sabab) to everything. Yet Dhu al-Qarnayn did not rely on what he had been given: he did not grow lax, nor did he become idle, but rather he took from God's bestowal to him a share of every means.

The sun setting in its place (the setting-point of the sun) is evidence that he was not in this place; rather, he was coming to it from the east. And what is meant by "the setting-place of the sun" (maghrib al-shams)? Does the sun set?

It sets in the eye of the beholder, at one place. If you observed the sun at sunset, you would find it setting, for example, in Giza. If you then went to Giza, you would find it setting at another place, and so on. So its setting means its disappearing from the sight of your eye, because the sun never truly disappears. It is always rising and setting: when it sets over one people, it rises over others. For this reason, the risings and the settings are multiple.

This gives us the continuous remembrance of God and its circulation on the tongues at all times. When we pray the noon prayer (zuhr), for example, others pray the afternoon prayer (asr), and still others pray the sunset prayer (maghrib), and so on. Thus Almighty God is remembered at every time by every time. The noon prayer does not end for God, nor does the afternoon prayer end for God, nor does the sunset prayer end for God. Rather, the proclamation of one of them never ceases throughout all the time and across the course of ages. For this reason the people of knowledge (ahl al-ma'rifa) say: "O time, in you is all of time."

Then He, exalted, says: ﴿And he found it setting in a muddy spring…﴾ (86). That is: in a spring that has water in it. We have said that "black mud molded" (al-hama' al-masnun) is the clay that has blackened from its abundance in the water. In verifying this matter, the scholar of India, Abu al-Kalam Azad, said, and the virtuous late Shaykh Abd al-Jalil Isa agreed with him, that it is at a place called "Izmir."

And His saying: ﴿And he found near it a people…﴾ (86). That is: near this spring.

﴿We said, O Dhu al-Qarnayn, either punish them or take in regard to them a good course﴾ (86).

So this is a delegation from God to him, and none is delegated except one trusted in disposal.

﴿Either punish them…﴾ (86): Surely they were disbelievers or idolaters who did not believe in a god. So either you seize them for their disbelief, or you take a good course regarding them.

But what is the goodness that God wants him to adopt? That is, they may be among the heedless to whom the call has not reached. So make clear to them the right course and guide them to God's religion. Whoever among them believes, treat him well; and whoever insists on his disbelief, punish him. So: you must first deal with them through good admonition and clear explanation, and then judge their conduct afterward.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 87:

His saying: ﴿Then We will punish him...﴾ [Surah al-Kahf 18:87]: This gives us an indication of the respite that He will give these people, a respite that enables him to admonish them, remind them, and make them understand the requirements of God's religion. We have already said that injustice (zulm) comes in various kinds, the most heinous and highest of which is associating partners with God (shirk), as the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, association with Him is great injustice﴾ [Surah Luqman 31:13].

Then the Exalted says: ﴿Then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with an unprecedented punishment﴾ [Surah al-Kahf 18:87]. That is: We will not punish him in proportion to what he did; rather, we will punish him only with a worldly penalty (ʿuqubah dunyawiyyah). This is because worldly penalties (al-ʿuqubat al-dunyawiyyah) were legislated to preserve the balance of society and to deter those who are not restrained by admonition. Otherwise, what is the benefit of admonition for one who is not a believer? Therefore we see nations that do not believe in God, nor in the Resurrection and the Hereafter, legislating these worldly penalties so that their affairs may be set right.

After the punishment of this world, its penalty here is a more severe punishment in the Hereafter: ﴿an unprecedented punishment﴾ [Surah al-Kahf 18:87]. The word nukr (unprecedented, unfamiliar) refers to that which we do not recognize and have no prior experience or familiarity with. This is because when we are punished in this world, we are punished in a manner within our natural capacity and endurance, whereas God's punishment in the Hereafter is something we do not recognize and is beyond our comprehension and capabilities.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 88:

His saying: ﴿So for him is the best reward﴾ (Surat al-Kahf): That is, We will give him a good reward.

﴿And We will speak to him of Our command with ease﴾ (Surat al-Kahf): We will speak to him words of goodness that encourage and motivate him, and if We assign him a task, We assign him a matter that is easy and not burdensome. This verse lays down for us the foundation of the process of reward, which is the balance of society and the cause of its advancement. A society without rewards that honor the diligent and punish the negligent is a society that ends in chaos and laxity, for if people feel safe from punishment, they become lazy. Perhaps what Egypt suffers from now of poor administration is due to the presence in society of individuals who are above the law, whom we cannot punish, so others become lax.

Likewise, we see ranks and prizes won by those who do not work, and won by those who ingratiate themselves, flatter, fawn and act hypocritically. These people have their crooked methods, which they excel at. As for the one who strives, works and is sincere, he is exhausted and busy perfecting and mastering his work; he has no time for these crooked methods. He draws near through his work and his excellence, and this is the one who deserves honor and deserves the prize. You can imagine the extent of corruption and laxity that this inverted, crooked picture causes. Therefore, the balance of society and the foundation of its advancement is: ﴿As for him who does wrong, We will punish him; then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him with a terrible punishment. But as for him who believes and does righteous work, he will have the best reward, and We will speak to him of Our command with ease﴾ (Surat al-Kahf). How good it is, then, that we set aside encouraging rewards and prizes, and hold ceremonies of honor for the outstanding and exemplary, provided that the balance of selection rests on truth and justice.

Al-husna (the best): the feminine superlative of husn (goodness). So if We give him al-husna, then the good is all the more so, and of this is His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who do good is the best reward and more﴾ (Surat Yunus).
Ibid: he went to another place.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 90:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Until, when he reached the rising-place of the sun﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): As we said regarding its setting-place, it is always rising, because it does not rise from one single place; rather, each people has a rising-place, and each has a setting-place, according to the breadth of the horizon.

Then the Exalted says: ﴿He found it rising over a people for whom We had made no shelter against it﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). The sitr (shelter) is the barrier between two things, and it is either to protect from the heat or to protect from the cold. Dhu al-Qarnayn went to a people of the nomadic (mutabbadin) who live naked, like some tribes in central Africa for example, or who have nothing to shield them from the sun, such as houses they live in, or trees they shade themselves under.

These are a people we call "dwellers in the open" (ḍāḥūn), meaning they have no shelter from the heat of summer or the cold of winter. They are backward, primitive people, not civilized. Such people, God the Exalted gives them, in their skins, what compensates them for these things they lack, so you find in their skins what grants them warmth in winter and coolness in summer.

We observe this in ordinary environments, where the human face, which is exposed to heat and cold and the changes of weather, is by nature of a particular constitution that bears these changes, unlike the rest of the body which is covered by clothing; if a part of it is uncovered, it becomes highly sensitive to heat or cold. Likewise among animals, some God has endowed with a special property in their skins that enables them to live in the frozen polar region without being affected by its cold.

These primitive people live in this way, adapting to their environment, and the matter of clothing does not occupy them, nor do they think about it, until civilized people come to them and show them clothing, and how it is an adornment and a covering of nakedness, so they adopt it.

We note here that the Qur'an has not told us anything about this people, or what Dhu al-Qarnayn did with them. If we consider the matter by analogy with the earlier people whom he met at the setting-place of the sun, we say: perhaps he attended to them and provided them with the means of advancement.

Some commentators hold that Dhu al-Qarnayn went to a place where its day lasts three months, or its daylight six months, so that on his arrival the sun was up, and he saw no setting for it in this place throughout his stay there, and saw no shelter that would screen it from them. It appears that he went to the far north.
Thus: that is, he went that way, just as he went to the west, he went to the east.
He went to another place.

The Sheikh al-Sha'rawi's commentary on surah 18, verse 93:

Al-sadd (السد): it is the barrier between two things. A barrier may be something immaterial, or it may be something natural and perceptible, such as mountains. Thus what is meant by "the two barriers" here is two mountains with a gap between them. Since He said "between the two barriers" (بين السدين), the word "between" (البين) here requires the existence of a gap between the two barriers through which the enemy comes.

﴿And found beneath them⋯ 93﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): that is, beneath them.

﴿a people who could hardly understand any speech 93﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): that is, they did not know speech and did not understand words, because whoever is able to understand is able to speak, and these people do not say anything, nor do they understand what is said to them. The meaning of:

﴿hardly⋯ 93﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): they do not come close to understanding, so it does not negate understanding from them entirely, but only mere closeness to understanding, as if there were no hope that they would be made to understand. However, the phrasing negates speech from them.

Then he said immediately after that:

﴿They said: O Dhul-Qarnayn...﴾ (18:93). So He affirmed speech for them?

It seems that he addressed them in the language of signs, and devised a way to make of their gestures a speech that he understood, and carried out for them what they wanted. There is no doubt that this process required from him effort and patience until he could make himself understood by them and understand them. Otherwise, he could have turned away from them on the pretext that they do not speak and do not communicate. So he is an example of the believing man, eager to do good, who spares no effort in benefiting the people and guiding them.

Signs have now become a well-known and recognized language, with its own rules and scholars who communicate through it, just as we now communicate with the mute.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 95:

The statement here is also one of indication and allusion, making them understand that he (Dhu al-Qarnayn) is independent of any wage, for with him is much of the good that God has given him. He only needs an active human force to assist him and to carry out this work with him.

From the verse we understand that the help a person who possesses the means on earth gives should be for the sake of God, and that the assistance should be of a kind that does not leave the one being helped in need of being helped at every moment. Rather, one should help him with an assistance that makes him independent of needing help afterwards, such as teaching him to work for himself instead of giving him, for example, money that he spends in his day and hour and then returns in need. Therefore they say: "Do not give me a fish, but teach me how to fish." In this way the assistance becomes continuous and lasting, having substance and having longevity.

Since Dhu al-Qarnayn was empowered on earth, and in his hand were much goodness and wealth, he had no need of money but of active human power. So he said: ﴿Help me with strength...﴾ [18:95], that is: with a strong, sincere human force and capacity.

﴿I will set up a barrier (radman) between you and them﴾ [18:95]. He did not say "sadd" (a solid barrier), because a solid barrier has the defect that if a shock occurs in one part of it, the other part shakes. Therefore he set up for them a radm (a layered embankment), meaning: he builds a wall in front and another behind, then places between them a radm of earth, so that the barrier is flexible and is not affected if an earthquake, for example, befalls it. Thus the earth within it is like the "sust" (shock absorber) that absorbs shocks.

Radm means placing layers of earth on top of one another until a pit is filled, for example, and levelled with the ground. From this is what we hear when someone rebukes his companion while he does not wish to listen, and says to him: "Bury this matter (irdam ʿala hadha al-mawdu')."

Dhu al-Qarnayn was not a wandering traveller who journeyed about alone in this way. Rather, God had granted him the means of everything, and this means that he was not by himself: with him were an army, power, numbers and equipment; with him were men and workers, with him were provisions and the necessities of the journey. He could have ordered his men to build this barrier, but he commanded the people and made them partners with him in the work, in order to train and teach them, for as long as they were able and had the human capacity required for this task.

God, blessed and exalted, says: ﴿God does not burden a soul beyond what He has given it﴾ (Surah al-Talaq, 65:7). So as long as your Lord has given you strength, act, and do not rely on others. For this reason you find here three commands: ﴿Help me with strength﴾, ﴿Bring me blocks of iron﴾, ﴿Bring me molten copper to pour over it﴾.

Zubar al-hadid (زبر الحديد): that is, large pieces of iron, its singular being zubrah. Al-qitr (القطر): this is molten copper. But how did Dhu al-Qarnayn build this barrier of iron and copper?

This construction resembles what engineers today do in architecture with iron and concrete; but he used iron, and he filled the gaps between it with molten copper so that it would be firmer, and so that the enemies could not breach it, and so that it would be smooth and even, and they could not climb it and ascend over it. As for His saying: ﴿until, when he had leveled between the two cliffs﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 18:96):

Al-sadafayn (الصدفين): the two sides, and from it is His saying, exalted be He: ﴿Who does greater wrong than one who denies the signs of God and turns away from them?﴾ (Surah al-An'am, 6:157); that is, he turned away from them to one side. So the meaning of "leveled between the two cliffs" is: he made the front and back walls level with the two mountains.

﴿He said, "Blow"﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 18:96): that is, on the iron which he had set alight, until the iron glowed, whereupon he called for the molten copper: ﴿He said, "Bring me molten copper to pour over it"﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 18:96). Thus he fused the glowing iron with the molten copper, and so we had a high, solid, smooth wall.

(That they could scale it): meaning, Gog and Magog were unable to climb over the barrier or scale it and pass through from its top, because it is smooth and slippery, with nothing on it to grip. ﴿And they could not pierce through it﴾ [18:97]: because it is hard.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 98:

Dhul-Qarnayn, who was a righteous man, did not fail to attribute the blessing to the First Bestower and to acknowledge that he was merely an intermediary and an instrument for carrying out the command of God: ﴿He said, "This is a mercy from my Lord. But when the promise of my Lord comes, He will make it level, and the promise of my Lord is ever true."﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) Because I took the means that God granted me and used them in the service of His servants. Thought is created by God, energy and power are created by God, and the materials and elements in nature are created by God. So how can I say: "I did such-and-such"?

Then God, the Exalted, says: ﴿When the promise of my Lord comes...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf), that is, the Hereafter.

﴿...He will make it level...﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): So beware lest you think that the solidity and strength of this dam will remain forever. This is only a work for the worldly life. When the promise of God of the Hereafter and the Resurrection comes, God will make it level and flatten it with the ground. That is so that they will not be deceived by it or act arrogantly toward others, after having been humiliated and oppressed by Gog and Magog. It is as though He is giving them a store of strength and a defense that protects them from tyranny after self-sufficiency.

﴿...and the promise of my Lord is ever true.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf): Certain and undoubtedly realized. The final verification concerning the matter of Dhul-Qarnayn and the building of the dam is that it is located in a place now called (Balkh), and the two mountains are from the Caucasus mountains, and they actually exist, and between them is a gap in which the structure was built. They say that the builder of this structure was Cyrus (Qurash), and this place is now between the Caspian Sea and the Black Sea.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1–53, fragments of 54–66) on surah 18, verse 99:

When the Resurrection comes, We will leave them surging against one another like the surging of water, such that you cannot separate them from one another, just as you cannot separate the droplets of water in the waves. Among them the cord-bearer will be mixed with the cord-bearer's counterpart (the sense: confusion, with everyone mixed together), the strong with the weak, and the fearful with the one who inspires fear. They are now in the station of the Resurrection, the worldly enmities have ended, and each person is occupied with himself.

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and We shall gather them together, a gathering﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:99). This is the second blast, because the first is the blast of swooning (al-sa'q), as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And the Trumpet will be blown, and whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth will swoon, except whom Allah wills. Then it will be blown again, and behold, they will be standing, looking on﴾ (Surah al-Zumar 39:68). So the first blast is the blast of swooning, and the second is the blast of resurrection and the Rising. Swooning may be deadly, and it may be a faint lasting for a period after which its subject revives. The deadly swoon is as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And in Thamud, when it was said to them, "Enjoy yourselves for a time." But they defied the command of their Lord, so the thunderbolt seized them while they were looking on﴾ (Surah al-Dhariyat 51:43–44). As for the stroke that causes fainting, it is like the one that befell Moses, peace be upon him, when he said: ﴿"My Lord, show me Yourself that I may look upon You." He said, "You will not see Me, but look at the mountain; if it remains in its place, then you will see Me." And when his Lord manifested Himself to the mountain, He made it crumble, and Moses fell unconscious. And when he awoke, he said, "Exalted are You! I have repented to You, and I am the first of the believers"﴾ (Surah al-A'raf 7:143). The firm, towering, solid mountain was crumbled when God manifested Himself to it, and Moses fell down swooning, unconscious. If Moses swooned from seeing the One who manifested Himself to him, how then would it be with seeing the One who manifests Himself, glorified be He?

It is as if the Truth, glorified be He, gave Moses, peace be upon him, an example, saying to him: "I am not withholding the vision from you, but before you see Me, look at the mountain first, so that it may be an example for you." Thus, the Qur'an does not prevent Allah from manifesting Himself to creation, but do we bear Allah's manifestation? 

By God's mercy toward us, He does not manifest Himself to us in the state we are in in this world. In the Hereafter, however, the Creator, glorified be He, will prepare us with a different preparation, and will create us with a creation suited to His manifestation, glorified be He, to the believers in the Hereafter, for He, glorified be He, said: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ (Surah al-Qiyamah 75:22–23). We shall observe this new preparation in all matters of the Hereafter; for example, there you will be nourished but will not defecate, because your nature in the Hereafter is different from your nature in this world.

Therefore, Moses's question, peace be upon him, came as a precise scientific question: ﴿"My Lord, show me Yourself, that I may look upon You..."﴾ (Surah al-A'raf 7:143). That is, show me how to look at You, for by my nature and constitution I cannot see You; rather, if You show Myself to me, then I will see.

In the light of this event of Moses, peace be upon him, we understand the hadith of the Prophet, peace and blessings of Allah be upon him: "Do not make distinctions among the prophets, for people will swoon on the Day of Resurrection, and I will be the first to be raised from the earth, and behold, Moses will be holding onto one of the pillars of the Throne. I do not know whether he was among those who swooned or whether he was compensated with the first swoon."

They said: because he swooned once in this world, and Allah does not combine two swoons upon His servant.

Its meaning: they are presented to them so that they see it and look upon it. This presentation is also for the believers, as in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And there is none of you but will pass over it﴾ (Surah Maryam: 71). Some people think that "wariduha" (واردها) means "entering it," but no, "wariduha" means: sees it and passes by it. Just as one says "warada al-ma'" (ترد الماء) meaning one reaches the water without drinking from it. That is because the Sirat, which will be laid over everyone, is set up over the back of Hell so that both the believer and the disbeliever can see it.

As for the believer, seeing the Fire before he enters Paradise shows him the extent of God's blessing upon him and His mercy toward him, in that He saved him from this punishment. He knows the virtue of faith upon him, and how He took him by the hand until he passed through this place safely. Therefore the Truth, glorified is He, reminds us of this matter, saying: ﴿So whoever is drawn away from the Fire and admitted into Paradise has certainly succeeded﴾ (Surah Al 'Imran: 185). As for the disbeliever, he will be presented to the Fire and will see it first, so his seeing it before entering it is the sight of regret, remorse, and terror, because he knows that he will enter it and will not escape from it. This matter has also appeared in Surah At-Takathur, where He, exalted is He, says: ﴿Competition in worldly gain distracts you, until you visit the graves. No! You are going to know. Then, no! You are going to know. No! If you knew with the certainty of knowledge, you would surely see Hellfire. Then you will surely see it with the eye of certainty. Then you will surely be questioned that Day about pleasure﴾ (Surah At-Takathur: 1-8). The meaning is: if you were to take from me the knowledge of certainty regarding what I inform you of the Fire and its punishment, you would be like one who has seen it, because I convey to you its true scientific picture. This is what we call 'ilm al-yaqin (knowledge of certainty, i.e., knowledge gained by report). But in the Hereafter you will see the Fire itself. This is 'ayn al-yaqin (the certainty of sight), that is, the actual picture that will be realized on the Day of Resurrection when you pass over the Sirat.

By God's mercy toward the believers, and by His bounty and generosity, the believer's relationship with the Fire ends at this point, and his salvation is decreed. Therefore, after this, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿Then you will surely be questioned that Day about pleasure﴾ (Surah At-Takathur: 8).

As for the disbeliever, may God forbid, he has a third stage with the Fire, which is 'haqq al-yaqin' (the truth of certainty), the day he enters it and directly experiences its heat, as He, exalted is He, said: ﴿But if he is of the deniers, the astray, then a welcome of boiling water, and burning in Hellfire. Indeed, this is the true certainty. So exalt the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾ (Surah Al-Waqi'ah: 92-96).

So: we have 'ilm al-yaqin, which is the scientific picture of the Fire, which the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, has informed us of, and that its attributes are such-and-such, and He warned us against it while we are in the ease and expanse of this world. 'Ayn al-yaqin: in the Hereafter when we pass over the Sirat and see the Fire with the sight of the eye. Then haqq al-yaqin: this is for the disbelievers when they are cast into it and directly experience it.

We have given an example for this: If I said to you: there is a city called New York, which has skyscrapers, that it lies on seven islands, and that its attributes are such-and-such, and I give you a true scientific picture of it, then if you believe me, this is 'ilm al-yaqin. If we pass over it by airplane and see it with the sight of the eye, this is 'ayn al-yaqin. If you land in it and tour through it, this is haqq al-yaqin.

So: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We will present Hell that Day to the disbelievers, a presentation﴾ (Surah Al-Kahf: 100) means: it is not like its presentation to the believers, but rather it is a presentation in which haqq al-yaqin is realized by entering it and directly experiencing it.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 101:

That is: over their eyes is a veil (ghishawah) that prevents them from perceiving sight. This is not all; rather: ﴿and they were not able to hear﴾ (Surat al-Kahf). What is meant here is hearing by which the listener benefits, the hearing of lesson and admonition. Otherwise their ears exist and are fit for hearing, and they do hear with them, but it is a hearing from which there is no benefit, because they recoil from hearing the truth and from hearing admonition, and they stop their ears against it. So in matters of good they are "an ear of clay and an ear of dough," as we say.

As for the believers, the Almighty, blessed and exalted is He, says of them: ﴿And when they hear what has been revealed to the Messenger, you see their eyes overflowing with tears because of what they have recognized of the truth﴾ (Surat al-Ma'idah, 83). So the aversion of those (disbelievers) to what they hear has made them as though they had no hearing, just as we say in our colloquial language: "You are ignoring me" (anta mutanish 'anni), meaning you do not want to hear. Among the sayings of the people of humor: a man said to his companion, "Is there in you someone who keeps a secret?" He said, "Yes." He said, "Give me a hundred pounds." He said, "As if I had not heard."

For this reason the Qur'an relates the saying of the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it, that perhaps you will overcome﴾ (Surat Fussilat, 26). That is: disrupt it, and do not give people the opportunity to hear it. Had they known that the Qur'an does not affect its hearer, they would not have said this. But with their Arab ears and their eloquent faculty, they know well that the Qur'an has an effect on its hearer, an effect that takes possession of the sides of his soul, and that he will surely recognize that it is inimitable, and that it is not the speech of men, and it will certainly call him to faith that this speech is the speech of God, and that Muhammad is the Messenger of God. Therefore some of them said to others, warning: ﴿Do not listen to this Qur'an, and make noise during it...﴾ (Surat Fussilat, 26).

In another verse the Almighty, blessed and exalted is He, says: ﴿Woe to every sinful liar, who hears the signs of God recited to him, then persists arrogantly as though he had not heard them. So give him the good news of a painful punishment﴾ (Surat al-Jathiyah, 7-8).

The matter may go beyond mere hearing to the prevention of speech, as in His saying: ﴿Has there not come to you the report of those before you, the people of Noah, 'Ad, and Thamud, and those after them, whom none knows but God? Their messengers came to them with clear proofs, but they put their hands over their mouths...﴾ (Surah Ibrahim, 9). So the matter is not only preventing hearing, but also preventing speech, for perhaps a word reaches their ears while they are attentive and it affects them. That is, they prevented themselves from speaking, as one says: "Be quiet," or "Shut your mouth."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 102:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do those who disbelieve think that they can take My servants as protectors besides Me?...﴾ [18:102]. That is, have they become blind to the truth, so that they think they can take My servants as protectors besides Me? We have already spoken about the word "servants" ('ibadi), and we said that they are those who believe in Me and love Me, who have chosen what God wills over the choices of their own souls. We also distinguished between "slaves" ('abid) and "servants" ('ibad).

The discussion here concerns those who disbelieved, who took as protectors besides God the servants of God who are brought near to Him and love Him, as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿The Messiah will never disdain to be a servant of God, nor will the angels brought near.…﴾ [4:172].

So how can you take them as protectors besides Me and oppose Me through them, when they are My beloved? He, the Exalted, says: ﴿And the Christians said, "The Messiah is the son of God."…﴾ [9:30].

Among them are those who said: "The angels are the daughters of God." So how can you take them as protectors besides God, when they do not disdain to be servants of God, and see their nobility and honour in their servitude to Him, glory be to Him? Yet behold, you take them as protectors besides Me. Would that you had made that toward My enemies! This is, on their part, a folly even in taking partners. Therefore their recompense is that We have prepared Hell for them: ﴿Indeed, We have prepared Hell for the disbelievers as a welcome [nuzul]﴾ [18:102]. The nuzul is what is prepared to honour a guest, such as hotels, for example. This is mockery of them and ridicule of them.

(قل) أي: يا محمد: ﴿Shall We inform you of the greatest losers in their deeds?﴾ (Surah al-Kahf)

Al-akhsar (الأخسر): an elative form (ism tafdil) from khasir (خاسر, "a loser"), so akhsar (الأخسر) means "greater in loss," i.e., those who suffer the most loss. (a'malan) (أعمالاً): i.e., their loss is because of their deeds.

Their striving has been lost because they do evil while thinking it is good, so they are astray from the very direction in which they think they are guided. An example of this is what we see in the deeds of disbelievers, who build hospitals, schools, and charitable and welfare associations, and who call for equality and other good values. They suppose by this that they have done well and offered good, but are these deeds done for Allah?

The reality is that they do them for people, for fame, and for history, so let them take their wages from people and from history, in honour, esteem, and immortalising of their memory.

The meaning of ﴿ضل سعيهم﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 104) is: it has become void, gone, as though it were nothing, like a mirage, as Allah the Exalted described them in His saying: ﴿And those who disbelieved, their deeds are like a mirage in a desert plain, which the thirsty one thinks is water until, when he comes to it, he finds it to be nothing﴾ (Surah an-Nur, 39). As for these people, Allah does not deprive them of their rights, nor does He withhold their reward, because they did well in the means; but this recompense takes place in this world, because when they worked and did well in the means, they worked for the world, and they have no share in the reward of the Hereafter. Allah the Exalted and Most High has clarified this matter in His saying: ﴿Whoever desires the tilth of the Hereafter, We increase for him in his tilth; and whoever desires the tilth of this world, We give him thereof, but he has no share in the Hereafter﴾ (Surah ash-Shura, 20). Nevertheless, the disbeliever retains his right, so it is not permitted for any of the believers to wrong him or transgress against him. In the hadith of our master Jabir ibn Abdullah (may Allah be pleased with him), he said: I heard that a narrator was narrating from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) a hadith, and I wished that I would not die, or that he would die, before I heard it from him. So I asked about him, and it was said: He has gone to Syria. He said: So I bought a she-camel, saddled her, and travelled for a month until I reached Syria. I asked about him, and it was said: He is Abdullah ibn Unays. So I went, and his servant said to him: Jabir ibn Abdullah is at the door. Jabir said: Ibn Unays came out, and he had stepped on his garments in his haste. Abdullah said: And they embraced.

So look at the precision of the scale and the justice of heaven, which safeguards the right of the disbeliever, so that it is avenged for him before he enters the Fire, even if his wrongdoer is a believer. And in His saying: ﴿their striving has been lost in the life of this world﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 104).

The word ḍalāl (going astray) has come in the Noble Qur'an in several usages, determined by the context in which it occurs. Ḍalāl may mean kufr (disbelief), which is the extreme of misguidance and the extreme of sins, as in the saying of the Blessed and Exalted Lord: ﴿Or do you wish to question your Messenger as Moses was questioned before? And whoever exchanges disbelief for faith has certainly strayed from the right way﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 108). Ḍalāl is also used to mean disobedience, even on the part of a believer, as in His saying: ﴿And it is not for a believing man or a believing woman, when Allah and His Messenger have decided a matter, that they should have any choice about their affair. And whoever disobeys Allah and His Messenger has certainly strayed into clear error﴾ (Surah al-Ahzab, 36). Ḍalāl is also used to mean being hidden in the earth, as in His saying: ﴿When we have become lost in the earth, will we indeed be in a new creation?﴾ (Surah as-Sajdah, 10); that is, we have become absent in it and concealed ourselves. Ḍalāl is also used to mean forgetfulness, as in His saying: ﴿That if one of them errs, the other will remind her﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah, 282). Ḍalāl also comes in the sense of heedlessness that befalls a person so that he falls into sin without intent, as in the story of Moses and Pharaoh, when Moses struck the man and killed him. When Pharaoh spoke to him he said: ﴿I did it then while I was among the astray﴾ (Surah ash-Shu'ara', 20); that is, he killed him in a state of heedlessness and without intent. And who knows that a blow kills? In reality the man came with the blow, not by it. It often happens that someone is run over by a car, and upon autopsy of the body it becomes clear that he died of a heart attack that coincided with the car accident.

Ḍalāl also comes in the sense of: not knowing the detail of a thing, as in His saying: ﴿And He found you unaware, so He guided you﴾ (Surah ad-Duha, 7); that is, he did not know what this was that his people were doing of disbelief.

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 105:

﴿Those who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf). The word "signs" (āyāt) is used in three senses, and they all disbelieved in and denied them. They disbelieved in the signs of the universe, which point to God's power, so they did not reflect on them or take heed from them. They disbelieved in the signs of the legal rulings, in the Qur'an, and in the message from the Messenger of God. Likewise, they disbelieved in the signs of the miracles that God sent to confirm the messengers, so they did not believe them. Therefore, the phrase ﴿Those who disbelieved in the signs of their Lord...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf) is general here, covering all these types.

(﴿And in His meeting...﴾): that is, they also disbelieved in meeting God on the Day of Resurrection and denied it. Some of them denied it completely, saying: ﴿When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?﴾ (Surat al-Mu'minun, 82).

Others acknowledged a resurrection according to their own desires, saying: ﴿And if I am returned to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a destination﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 36).

Some said that the resurrection is of the spirit without the body, and they said a great deal about this. So either they deny the resurrection, or they portray it in a form that is not the reality.

Then God says: ﴿Their deeds have become worthless...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 105). That is, they were nullified and their benefit was lost. ﴿So We will not assign for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 105). The orientalists have objected to this verse, saying: ﴿So We will not assign for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 105).

They said: How can we reconcile this with the verses that affirm the scale, as in God's saying: ﴿And We will set up the scales of justice for the Day of Resurrection, and no soul will be wronged in the least. And even if it is the weight of a mustard seed, We will bring it forth. And sufficient are We as reckoners﴾ (Surat al-Anbiya', 47).

And His saying: ﴿So he will be in a pleasant life. But as for one whose scales are light, his refuge will be an abyss. And what can make you know what it is? It is a blazing Fire﴾ (Surat al-Qari'ah, 7-11).

We say: The scholars, in reconciling these verses, said: The meaning of God's saying ﴿So We will not assign for them on the Day of Resurrection any weight﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 105) is that it came in the manner of contempt and disregard. The meaning is that they have no weight with Us, that is, no consideration. We use this same meaning today, saying: "So-and-so has no weight with me," meaning: "He has no value."

When you reflect on this verse and contemplate it, you find that the noble Qur'an says: ﴿So We will not assign for them...﴾ (Surat al-Kahf, 105).

It does not say "against them" (ʿalayhim). Therefore, the scale exists, but it is not in their favor. The meaning is: We will not set up a scale for them, but We will set up a scale against them.

(That is, what has been said about the nullifying of their deeds, and our giving them no weight, is not an injustice on our part or wrong done to them, but a recompense for their disbelief. So His words ﴿because they disbelieved﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) mean: because of their disbelief.)

﴿And they took My signs and My messengers in mockery﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). They mocked the signs of God, and whenever they heard a verse they said: "Fables of the ancients."

﴿When Our verses are recited to him, he says, "Fables of the ancients!"﴾ (Surah al-Qalam).

Likewise, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was not spared their derision and mockery, and the Qur'an relates their words to the Messenger of God: ﴿O you to whom the Reminder has been sent down, indeed you are a madman!﴾ (Surah al-Hijr).

Their saying ﴿to whom the Reminder has been sent down﴾ (Surah al-Hijr), meaning the Qur'an, while they do not believe in it, is mockery and derision. In Surah al-Munafiqun the Qur'an says of them: ﴿They are the ones who say, "Do not spend on those who are with the Messenger of God until they disperse."﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun).

Their saying ﴿the Messenger of God﴾ (Surah al-Munafiqun) is not an affirmation of faith in him, but either heedlessness on their part regarding the lie they practice, or mockery and derision, as when you are in a gathering and see one of them claiming knowledge and feigning it, and you say: "Ask this scholar."

In another verse, He, glory be to Him, says concerning their mockery of the Messenger of God: ﴿And indeed, those who disbelieve would almost make you slip with their eyes when they hear the Reminder, and they say, "Indeed, he is a madman!"﴾ (Surah al-Qalam).

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 107:

His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who believe... [107]﴾ (Surah al-Kahf).

We have said before that faith (iman) is the correction of the emotional and doctrinal wellspring, so that actions issue in a manner fitting your faith in the One who legislated. From here, faith comes first and is a condition for the acceptance of deeds. Otherwise, there are those who do good not from a standpoint of faith but for other considerations, and intention is a necessary condition for the acceptance of a deed.

For this reason, God Most High punishes whoever works for other than God. He punishes him by having the one he served deny him, reject him, and hate him because of it, instead of acknowledging his favor. From here they said: "Beware the evil of the one to whom you have shown kindness." This is a sound saying, because when you do good to a person, you crush his pride, and your hand becomes the upper hand over him. If he obtains a share of life and becomes a person of standing among people, and if he is not of a balanced soul, he does not love the one who bestowed favor upon him on some day that crushed his pride. Therefore you see him hating your existence and not wanting to see you, and he may plot schemes against you so that you disappear from his path and leave the field to him, because you are the only one whose presence embarrasses him.

Therefore, whoever does a deed for other than God, God leaves him to the one for whom he did it, so that he takes his reward from him. The reward then comes contrary to what you expected: you did it for him so that he would honor you, and he humiliates you; you did it so that he would respect you, and he belittles you; you did it so that he would befriend you, and he becomes your enemy. Therefore they say: "Working for God brings swift reward, while working for other than God has no guaranteed outcome; it may repay you, or it may not."

Then the Truthful, Glorified One followed faith with righteous deeds, because righteous deeds must proceed from faith and issue from it. He, Exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, those who believe and do righteous deeds... [107]﴾ (Surah al-Kahf).

﴿and do righteous deeds... [107]﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) means: doing a thing that is good. If the thing is good in itself, then one leaves it in its goodness, not corrupting it, or one increases its goodness, like a well of water from which people drink. Either you leave it in its state of goodness, not casting into it what blocks or corrupts it and thus takes the good out of its goodness, or you increase its goodness by adding what improves its performance and increases its efficiency, such as building a wall around it to protect it, or a covering to preserve it, or a lifting device that makes its use easier for people.

When an individual does righteous deeds, his yield from the goodness of others is greater than his yield from his own deed, because he is one individual, and he benefits from the goodness of the whole society. Therefore, the commands of the Lawgiver should not seem burdensome to you, for He takes from you in order to give to you, and secures your life at the time of need and want. When this social solidarity is available to you, you receive life with a contented soul in ease and with a tranquil soul in hardship.

When the Shari'ah commands you to sponsor the orphan and honor him, it reassures you about your children after you, so do not grieve if some harm befalls you, because you are in a cooperative society that will sponsor your children. Indeed, the orphan under Islam and its teachings may have a happier lot than he would have in the care of his father, because upon the death of his father he finds all the believers as fathers to him, whereas his father, in his lifetime, may have been preoccupied with other things and not benefited him at all, and may even have turned people away from doing good to him, as people say: "His father is alive and he is taking care of him."

Therefore Ahmad Shawqi says:

"The orphan is not the one whose two parents have passed away;
Rather the orphan is the one who, having lost both, is left humiliated to the cares of life,
Whether his mother has abandoned him, or his father is preoccupied."

His saying, Most High: ﴿They shall have the Gardens of Paradise as their lodging [107]﴾ (Surah al-Kahf).

Al-Firdaws: it is the highest part of Paradise. Al-Nuzl: what a person prepares to honor his guest, of lodging, the necessities of life and its luxuries. When a person prepares lodging for his guest, he prepares it according to his capabilities, his means, and his knowledge of things. So what about when the one preparing the lodging is God, blessed and exalted?

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 108:

The eternity of bliss in the Hereafter distinguishes it from the bliss of this world, however lofty the latter may be. Worldly bliss comes in proportion to our conception of bliss and according to our capacities. Even if we reach the peak of enjoyment in this world, we live in constant fear of its loss: either bliss leaves you, or you leave it. In Paradise, however, the blessing is everlasting, neither cut off nor forbidden, and you abide in it forever, so the blessing will never leave you and you will never leave it.

Therefore, the Exalted says after this: ﴿They will not desire any transfer from it.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf 18:108), meaning: they will not seek to be moved away from it to anything else, for there is no conceivable bliss higher than this.

It is well known that a human being has recreational ambitions: whenever he attains some good, he aspires to something higher, and whenever he obtains a pleasure, he seeks more of it. This is the case in this world, but in the Hereafter the matter is different. Otherwise, how could one seek a bliss higher than Paradise, about which God said: ﴿Whenever they are provided with a fruit from it as provision, they say: "This is what we were provided with before," and they are given it in semblance...﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:25), meaning: whenever God provides them with a fruit, another one comes to them, and they say: "We were provided with its like before," and they think it is like the previous one. But it is not like the previous one; rather it has a new and different taste, even if it is the same fruit. This is because the power of causes is limited, whereas the power of the Causer is not limited.

The Truth, glory be to Him, is able to bring forth for you one fruit in a thousand colors and a thousand tastes, because His perfect attributes, in their power, are without end. Therefore He says: ﴿And they will be given it in semblance...﴾ (Surah al-Baqarah 2:25). The fruit is one and similar in appearance, but its taste differs.

A person among us, in order to make his way in life, keeps learning, to obtain a certificate, for example, or to learn a trade, and remains in toil and hardship for about twenty-five years of his life, hoping to live the rest of his presumed life at ease and contentment. Suppose you will live the rest of your life in comfort: how much of it will remain?

As for the eternal rest in the Hereafter, it is a time without end, and a everlasting bliss that never ends. So for what could a person still yearn after all this? And to what could he aspire?

Because His power has no limits, and since His power has no limits, the things He decrees are likewise without limit. Therefore, even if the sea were ink (midad), meaning ink with which the words of Allah are written, which are (kun) ("Be!") that bring the decreed things into existence, it would not suffice for the words of Allah. ﴿And even if We brought the like of it as a supplement﴾ (Surah al-Kahf, 18:109).

We say, for example, about a good product: the factory cannot produce anything better than this. But the creation of Allah does not stop at a limit, because a factory works on existing materials, whereas the Truth, blessed and exalted is He, creates things by the word "Kun." Therefore, in the finest hotels of the world, the utmost that science has reached in serving people is that you press a certain button, and whatever you want of food or drink comes out for you.

Undoubtedly, these things are prepared and equipped in advance; they are only summoned by pressing a button specific to each kind. But is there any bliss in this world that brings you what you want the moment it occurs to your mind? Thus, the bliss of this world has limits at which it ends. Therefore the Truth, glorified and exalted is He, says: ﴿Until, when the earth takes on its adornment and is beautified, and its people think they have power over it, Our command comes to it by night or by day, and We make it a harvested field as if it had not flourished yesterday. Thus do We detail the signs for a people who give thought﴾ (Surah Yunus, 10:24). It is as if Allah, glorified is He, is saying to us: You have exhausted your means in this world and reached the utmost of its enjoyments and adornments, so come to what I have prepared for you. Leave behind what you were in of the means of Allah; come and live by Allah. You were in the world of causes, so come to the One who causes.

Although the Truth, glorified is He, spoke in this verse of the ink with which the words of Allah are written, He spoke of the pens with which they are written in another verse, in more detail on this matter, saying: ﴿And if whatever trees are on the earth were pens and the sea, with seven more seas to supply it, the words of Allah would not be exhausted...﴾ (Surah Luqman, 31:27).

Here we pause at the precision of the Qur'anic expression. If we imagine all the trees on the earth as pens, together with the trees' distinctive continual renewal and constant recurrence, which makes them a wealth without measure and without end, and we imagine the water of the sea as ink with which to write, the sea's water since Allah created it is nonetheless limited, fixed, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, since the trees renew and recur while the sea's water is fixed and does not increase, He, glorified is He, said: ﴿And the sea, with seven more seas to supply it...﴾ (Surah Luqman, 31:27), so that the increase of water is proportionate to the increase of trees. What is meant is seven times its like, and He specifically chose this number because it is the highest number among the Arabs.

Science has also clarified the cycle of water in nature, and from it we know that the quantity of water on earth is fixed and does not increase, because the water that is consumed evaporates and returns anew. A human being, for example, if he drank a hundred tons of water over his lifetime, then calculate what comes out of him of urine, sweat and waste in the process of elimination, and you will find it the same quantity he drank, which has evaporated and taken up its cycle anew. Therefore they say: "A single sip of water that Adam drank has become millions."

Commentary of al-Sha'rawi (Tafsir al-Sha'rawi, surahs 1-53, fragments of 54-66) on surah 18, verse 110:

﴿Say﴾ i.e., O Muhammad. This is a new statement. ﴿Say: I am only a human being like you.﴾ (Surah al-Kahf)

That is: take me as an example. I am not an angel; I am only a human being like you. I held myself to the method that I demand of you. I do not order you to do anything while I myself stray from it. Rather, on the contrary, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was the least of people in his share of the pleasures and adornments of life.

Among those who believed in him were the wealthy who enjoyed the finest foods and wore the most expensive clothes, while the Messenger of God (ﷺ) would pass a month or two months without a fire being lit in his house for food. He wore patched garments. Moreover, his children did not inherit from him as the rest of people inherit, and they were not permitted to receive zakat as others were. Thus they were deprived of a right that others enjoyed.

Therefore the Messenger of God (ﷺ) was ﴿adna al-aswat﴾ (the lowest of voices), i.e., the least of those present in the enjoyments and adornments of life. This draws our attention to the fact that the message did not bring Muhammad any worldly benefit, and did not distinguish him from others in the fleeting splendour of this world. Rather, what distinguished him was in values and virtues.

From here, the Messenger of God (ﷺ) used to say: "Something is conveyed to me, i.e., from above, and I say: I am not like you; and something is taken from me, and I say: I am only a human being like you."

The verse here does not distinguish him (ﷺ) from mankind except in that ﴿it is revealed to me﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). So Muhammad differed from mankind only in that revelation was made to him. Then the Exalted says: ﴿Your God is only one God﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). ﴿Innama﴾ (only) is a particle of restriction. ﴿Your God is one God﴾ means: there is no god but Him. This is the summit of matters, so do not turn to any other god. Among the greatest blessings of God upon man is that he has one God. The Truth, glorified is He, has struck for us an example to clarify this matter, saying:

﴿God has struck an example: a man in whom are partners quarrelling, and a man belonging entirely to one man. Are the two equal in comparison?﴾ (Surah al-Zumar, 29)

A slave owned by several masters who pull him in different directions is not equal to a slave owned by one master, because they quarrel and disagree among themselves and he is perplexed among them; if this one is pleased, that one is angered. Is he equal to a slave belonging to a single master? Thus, among the things for which God is to be praised is that He is one God.

﴿So whoever hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾ (Surah al-Kahf).

People do good for aims that God has set for them as reward, and among these aims is Paradise and its delights. But this verse makes clear to us an aim higher than Paradise and its delights: it is meeting God, the Exalted, and looking upon His noble Face. So His saying, the Exalted, ﴿hopes for the meeting with his Lord﴾ (Surah al-Kahf) turns attention away from the blessing to the Bestower, blessed and exalted is He. Whoever wishes the meeting with his Lord, not merely His reward in the Hereafter:

﴿let him do righteous work﴾ (Surah al-Kahf). This is the means to meeting God, because righteous work is evidence that you have respected the command of the One who commands it, and have trusted His wisdom and His love for you, so your soul is at ease in the shade of His obedience. Then when you retire to your bed and review the film of your deeds, you find nothing but good, which makes your soul happy and your breast expand, and you do not fear evil from anyone, nor fear the outcome of a matter whose end is not praiseworthy. Who is it that has bestowed upon you all these blessings and enabled you to them? Then: ﴿and let him not associate anyone in the worship of his Lord﴾ (Surah al-Kahf).

We have said before: Paradise is one of the things, so do not associate anything in the worship of God, even if that thing is Paradise. You must elevate your aims, not to Paradise but to the meeting with its Lord, its Creator, and the One who bestowed it upon you.

We have given an example of this: a man who prepared a great feast with the finest foods and drinks and invited his beloved ones. When they entered, the food occupied them all except one, who was not concerned with the food and drink, and asked about the host so that he might greet him and be at ease with him.

How true are the words of Rabi'a al-'Adawiyya:

They all worship out of fear, or in hope that they may dwell in the gardens and obtain them.
I have no share in the Gardens or the Fire;
and they consider salvation a great share in palaces, and drinking from Salsabil.
I do not seek any substitute for my love.

This explains to us the sacred hadith: "Had I not created Paradise and Hellfire, would I not still be worthy to be worshipped?"

The servant should not be utilitarian even in worship, and the Truth, glorified is He, is worthy of worship in Himself, neither out of fear of His Fire nor out of desire for His Paradise. So, O God, grant us this station, and make us, by Your mercy, among its people.
